lib/main.dart.overview: The application entry point. It opens the persisted `SettingsStore`, constructs the one global `AppState`, mounts it with Provider and then starts account connection and AI discovery. The `HearthmailApp` widget defines the Material 3 theme for light and dark mode and picks the first screen: account setup on first run, the inbox otherwise. This is the file behind tour step 2.

sections.title: Bootstrap and global state
sections.explanation: `main()` calls `WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized()` first because `SettingsStore.open()` uses platform plugins before `runApp`. A single `AppState` is created and provided with `ChangeNotifierProvider.value`, so every widget below can `watch`/`read` it. The tour describes this as a post-frame callback, but the code does not call `addPostFrameCallback`. It calls `runApp` and then awaits `state.init()`. `init()` yields at its first `await`, so Flutter can paint the first frame while IMAP connects. **Note:** the `material_ui` import (instead of `package:flutter/material.dart`) is a dependency declared in pubspec.yaml. Readers used to stock Flutter should know it is the source of `MaterialApp`, `ThemeData`, etc. here. Also, `.value` means Provider will not dispose `AppState`. Its timers and connections live for the whole process.

sections.title: Theme construction
sections.explanation: `buildTheme` is static so the light and dark themes come from one seed colour (`0xFF5B5BD6`) via `ColorScheme.fromSeed`. It turns on Material 3 and a compact visual density suited to a dense desktop mail client. It flattens the app bar (no elevation or scroll tint) and makes snack bars float at a fixed 420 px width, which the app uses for its toast and "Undo send" messages.

sections.title: Root widget and first-run routing
sections.explanation: `context.select<AppState, bool>` rebuilds `MaterialApp` only when "has at least one account" changes, not on every `notifyListeners()` from the busy `AppState`. That narrow subscription matters because `AppState` notifies very often (loading, sorting, indexing). Routing is done by swapping `home` instead of using a navigator. Adding the first account therefore replaces `AccountSetupPage(isFirstRun: true)` with `HomePage` automatically.

analysis_options.yaml.overview: Static-analysis configuration for `flutter analyze` and IDEs. It adopts the standard `flutter_lints` rule set and excludes native platform folders and build output from analysis. The project adds no custom lint rules beyond the recommended set. It is part of the entry-point and packages step of the tour.

sections.title: Recommended lint set
sections.explanation: The header comments come from the Flutter template. The meaningful line is `include: package:flutter_lints/flutter.yaml`, which pulls in Flutter's recommended lints (the `flutter_lints` dev dependency in pubspec.yaml). Any warning you see in the IDE comes from this shared rule set, not from project-specific rules.

sections.title: Excluded paths
sections.explanation: `build/**` and the native runner folders (`android`, `ios`, `windows`, `macos`) are excluded from analysis. They contain generated or platform code, and including them would only add noise and slow the analyzer. Dart files in `lib/`, `test/` and `tool/` stay fully analyzed.

sections.title: Linter customization (unused)
sections.explanation: The `rules:` map has only commented-out examples, so the project runs the recommended set unchanged. The comments recommend suppressing rules locally with `// ignore:` instead of disabling them project-wide, which keeps the baseline strict. Because the `rules:` key has no entries, it parses as null. That is harmless, but you would add entries here to tighten style (for example `prefer_single_quotes`).

macos/Runner/Release.entitlements.overview: The macOS App Sandbox entitlements used for release builds. Each key grants a capability that a feature depends on: outgoing network for IMAP/SMTP, OAuth and Ollama, an incoming network listener for the OAuth loopback redirect, and file access for attachments. It matches the debug entitlements, so features behave the same when signed for distribution (tour step 14).

sections.title: Property-list header
sections.explanation: A standard Apple property list. Xcode reads it at code-signing time and embeds the keys in the app's signature. Changing it requires a rebuild and re-sign. It is not read at runtime by Dart code.

sections.title: Network entitlements
sections.explanation: `network.client` lets the sandboxed app open outbound sockets for IMAP/SMTP, the OAuth token endpoints and the local Ollama server at `localhost:11434`. Without it, `AppState.friendlyError` would surface the "Operation not permitted" sandbox message. `network.server` is needed because OAuth sign-in runs a short-lived loopback HTTP server to catch the redirect. **Risk note:** a server entitlement in a release build is a broader permission, so the loopback listener should bind only to 127.0.0.1 and close promptly. That logic lives in `lib/services/oauth.dart`.

sections.title: Sandbox and file access
sections.explanation: `app-sandbox` is mandatory for Mac App Store distribution and confines the app to its container. `files.user-selected.read-write` allows reading files chosen in an open/save panel (adding attachments via `file_selector`). `files.downloads.read-write` lets `AppState.saveAttachment` write straight into `~/Downloads` without a dialog.

sections.title: Closing tags
sections.explanation: End of the dictionary and plist. Keep this file in sync with `DebugProfile.entitlements`. A capability present only in debug is a classic source of "works in development, fails in release" bugs.

test/widget_test.dart.overview: Despite its template name, this file holds pure unit tests with no widgets, network, mail server or Ollama. It pins down the deterministic helpers the app relies on: `SearchPlan` query generation and lenient parsing, HTML-to-text conversion, remote-image blocking, cleanup of AI drafts, address parsing and Markdown-to-plain conversion. It is part of tour step 15's "test the pure logic" strategy.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Imports only the model and service libraries under test via `package:hearthmail/...`. No Flutter widget or `AppState` import is needed. This is why these tests run quickly and without a device.

sections.title: SearchPlan: IMAP, Gmail and JSON
sections.explanation: The first test fixes the exact IMAP SEARCH string. Multiple keywords become nested `OR TEXT` terms, dates use IMAP's `d-Mon-yyyy` format and unread maps to `UNSEEN`. The equivalent Gmail `X-GM-RAW` query is checked too. The second test covers quote escaping (`\"`) and that an empty plan becomes `ALL`, which prevents malformed server commands. The third shows that `fromJson` tolerates messy model output: blank keywords, empty strings, the literal `'null'` and unparseable dates are all dropped instead of throwing. That matters because the plan comes from an LLM.

sections.title: HTML helpers
sections.explanation: `htmlToText` must keep list structure (`- One`) and drop `<style>` contents, because the AI and the vector index read this text. `blockRemoteImages` must strip remote (tracking-pixel) images while keeping `cid:` inline images that are embedded in the message itself. That is the privacy rule from the safe-rendering step.

sections.title: Draft cleanup and address parsing
sections.explanation: `EmailAi.cleanDraft` removes the chatter that local models often add ("Here's a draft:", a `Subject:` line, code fences) so only the body reaches the composer. `MailService.parseAddresses` accepts both `,` and `;` separators and display names. `markdownToPlain` produces the text/plain alternative for outgoing mail. These are string contracts, so exact-equality assertions are appropriate here.

lib/models/account_config.dart.overview: Defines `AccountConfig`, the serializable connection settings for one IMAP/SMTP account, and `ProviderPreset`, a small catalogue of well-known providers. Secrets are deliberately not part of this model: passwords and OAuth tokens live in the keychain through `SettingsStore`. This is one of the shared domain models from tour step 4, used by setup, `MailService` and `AppState`.

sections.title: AuthType and constructor
sections.explanation: `AuthType` separates app-password accounts from Google/Microsoft OAuth. `AppState._credentialsFor` switches on it to build either `PasswordCredentials` or `OAuthCredentials`. The `const` constructor defaults to implicit-TLS ports (IMAP 993, SMTP 465), so most configs need only hosts and email. The doc comment states the key security decision: the password is never in this object.

sections.title: Fields and derived getters
sections.explanation: All fields are `final`, which makes the config an immutable value. To edit an account you replace it. `loginName` falls back to the email when no separate username is set. The TLS getters encode a port convention: SMTP uses STARTTLS on anything other than 465, and IMAP uses STARTTLS only on 143. A non-standard port, such as SMTP over implicit TLS on a custom port, would be misclassified. `isGmail` uses a host substring check. `AppState` uses it, for example, to skip indexing Sent mail because Gmail's All Mail already contains it.

sections.title: JSON serialization
sections.explanation: `toJson`/`fromJson` round-trip the non-secret fields. `authType` is stored by enum `name`. `fromJson` is defensive: missing optional fields fall back to defaults, and an unknown `authType` string falls back to `password` via `orElse`, so old settings files keep loading. Required fields (`id`, `email`, hosts) are cast directly and will throw if they are absent, so a corrupt entry fails loudly rather than producing a half-empty account.

sections.title: Provider presets
sections.explanation: `ProviderPreset` holds the server settings and user-facing help for Gmail, iCloud, Fastmail and Yahoo. The help text explains the provider's app-password requirement and links to the page where you create one, which is the most common stumbling block for IMAP clients. Only iCloud overrides the SMTP port (587, STARTTLS). `all` is a `const` list, so presets cost nothing at runtime.

sections.title: Lookup by email domain
sections.explanation: `forEmail` takes the domain after the last `@`, lowercases it and finds the first preset that claims it. It returns `null` for unknown domains, and the setup page then falls back to autoconfig discovery or manual entry. A linear scan is fine for four presets.

lib/services/ai/ollama_provider.dart.overview: The concrete `AiProvider` that talks to a local Ollama server over HTTP. It implements model listing (`/api/tags`), streaming chat with optional JSON-schema output (`/api/chat`) and batched embeddings (`/api/embed`). It also translates connection and HTTP failures into user-readable `AiException`s. It is the middle tier of the pluggable AI layer in tour step 5, and every AI feature and the semantic index go through it.

sections.title: Construction and shared settings
sections.explanation: The base URL defaults to `http://localhost:11434`, so no email content leaves the machine. An `http.Client` can be injected for testing. `contextTokens` is fixed at 8192 for every request on purpose: Ollama reloads a model when `num_ctx` changes, so a constant window avoids slow reloads between features. `_uri` strips trailing slashes from a user-entered base URL to avoid `//api/...` paths.

sections.title: Listing installed models
sections.explanation: A cheap `GET /api/tags` with a 5-second timeout serves as both health check and model discovery. `AppState.refreshAi` calls it at startup and when settings change. `SocketException` and `TimeoutException` become friendly messages ("Is the Ollama app running?"). Names are sorted so pickers are stable. A malformed body would throw a raw cast error instead of an `AiException`.

sections.title: Streaming chat
sections.explanation: `chat` is an `async*` generator that yields text chunks as they arrive, so UI like `AiStreamView` can render progressively. The request disables `think` (hidden reasoning is slow and not needed for email tasks) and sets `keep_alive: 30m` to keep the model warm. `'format': ?jsonSchema` uses Dart's null-aware map element: the key is included only when a schema is passed. Ollama then constrains output to that JSON schema. The response is newline-delimited JSON. Each line is decoded, `error` objects are raised and the loop stops on `done`. **Risk:** unlike the other calls there is no timeout, so a stalled server leaves the stream waiting until the consumer cancels it.

sections.title: Batch embeddings
sections.explanation: `embed` sends many inputs in one `/api/embed` call with `truncate: true`, so long emails are cut by the server instead of failing. It uses a generous 2-minute timeout because indexing batches (16 emails at a time from `AppState`) can be slow on modest hardware. It returns `List<List<double>>` converted from JSON numbers. `VectorIndex` later truncates and normalizes them.

sections.title: Error text and cleanup
sections.explanation: `_errorText` parses Ollama's error JSON. It recognizes the common "model not found" case and turns it into an actionable hint (`ollama pull <model>`). Any parse failure falls back to the bare HTTP status. `close()` releases the HTTP client. `AppState.refreshAi` closes the old provider before creating a new one when the URL changes.

lib/services/vector_index.dart.overview: A tiny per-account vector database for semantic search. It stores one normalized embedding per email in memory and in a compact custom binary file, and answers queries by an exact cosine-similarity scan. `EmbeddingFormat` adds the task prefixes each embedding model expects for queries and documents. This file is the core of the "semantic" tier in tour step 9. `AppState` fills it in the background and fuses its hits with IMAP results.

sections.title: Imports and IndexedMail
sections.explanation: `IndexedMail` holds just enough to fetch a hit again from the server: a stable `key`, the folder `path`, the IMAP `uid` and a `date`. The date is used to evict the oldest mail. Message bodies are not stored, so a search hit costs one `fetchByUids` round trip, but the index file stays small.

sections.title: Design, limits and lookups
sections.explanation: The class comment states the design choice: at 20,000 emails × 512 dims (~40 MB), a brute-force scan takes about 10 ms. That beats approximate indexes like HNSW on both accuracy and simplicity. `dims = 512` relies on Matryoshka-style models where leading dimensions carry most meaning, a choice measured in `tool/model_bench.dart`. Storage is parallel lists (`_entries`, `_vectors`) plus a `_pos` key→index map for O(1) `contains`. `oldestIn` and `countIn` are linear scans, which is fine at this size.

sections.title: Normalize, add, remove, search
sections.explanation: `_prepare` truncates to `dims` and L2-normalizes, so similarity becomes a plain dot product. Zero vectors are left as zeros to avoid division by zero. `add` upserts by key. `remove` swaps the last element into the hole (O(1) delete) and fixes its `_pos`, so insertion order is not preserved. `search` scores every vector, keeps those at or above `minScore`, sorts descending and returns Dart record tuples `(IndexedMail, double)`. `AppState` uses thresholds measured for embeddinggemma (0.25 for candidates, 0.4 for "related" keyword-search extras).

sections.title: Binary save with eviction
sections.explanation: `scheduleSave` debounces bursts of `add` calls into one write after 3 s. `save` first evicts the oldest entries beyond `maxEntries`. It then writes a little-endian format: magic `LMVI`, version 1, the model name, then per entry key/path/uid/int64 millis/float32 vector. It writes to `.tmp` and `rename`s, which makes the replace atomic and protects against a half-written file. **Gotchas:** `_dirty` is cleared before eviction, which calls `remove` and sets it again, so the next scheduled save rewrites the file unnecessarily. `_dirty` is also cleared before the write, so a failed write is not retried until the index changes. Two overlapping `save()` calls would share the same `.tmp` path.

sections.title: Loading and deleting
sections.explanation: `open` sanitizes the account id into a filename under the app-support directory and parses the format with small `u32`/`str` closures over a `ByteData` cursor. A wrong magic number, a wrong version or a **different model name** returns an empty index: vectors from different models are not comparable, so a model switch silently triggers re-indexing. Any parse error clears everything ("a damaged index only costs re-indexing"). That is a sensible failure mode for a cache. `delete` cancels the pending save and removes the file, for account removal and "Rebuild index".

sections.title: EmbeddingFormat prompts
sections.explanation: Embedding models are trained with specific task prefixes. `EmbeddingFormat` detects the model family by name (embeddinggemma, qwen3-embedding, nomic) and wraps queries and documents accordingly. Unknown models get raw text. Documents are compacted to one line, capped at 1500 body characters, and include sender and ISO date, so queries like "invoice from Chase last month" can match on metadata as well as content.

lib/ui/widgets/ai_widgets.dart.overview: Three reusable widgets that give AI output a consistent look: `MarkdownText` renders the small Markdown subset the models produce, `AiStreamView` shows a model's streamed answer as it arrives, and `AiCard` is the tinted container that marks content as AI-generated. They appear in the reading pane (summaries, Catch me up) and elsewhere, as described in tour step 10.

sections.title: Inline bold parsing
sections.explanation: `MarkdownText.inline` splits a line on a non-greedy `**...**` regex into plain and semi-bold `TextSpan`s. It is a static helper so other widgets can reuse it. It handles only bold. Italics, links and code are rendered literally. That is a deliberate scope limit: the prompts ask models for simple formatting, and a full Markdown renderer would be heavier and more permissive.

sections.title: Line-based Markdown layout
sections.explanation: `build` works line by line. Blank lines become small spacers. Lines matching `-`, `*`, `•` or `1.` become a `Row` with a bullet or number and wrapped text, indented when the marker is not at the line start. `#` headings become semi-bold text. Everything is wrapped in a `SelectionArea` so users can select and copy parts of an AI answer. The bullet regex requires whitespace after the marker, so a line starting with `**bold**` is not mistaken for a bullet.

sections.title: AiStreamView
sections.explanation: Takes a `start` factory rather than a stream, and calls it once in `initState`, so the request is not re-issued on rebuilds. Chunks are appended to a `StringBuffer` with `setState`, and the subscription is cancelled in `dispose`, which stops the HTTP stream when the card closes. Errors are shown inline in the theme's error colour, and a Copy button appears only once the stream is done. `onDone` lets callers capture the final text, for example to cache a summary. **Gotcha:** there is no `didUpdateWidget`, so passing a new `start` to an existing widget does nothing. Callers must change the widget's `key` to restart generation.

sections.title: AiCard
sections.explanation: A full-width container tinted with `primaryContainer` at 35% opacity, with a sparkle (`auto_awesome`) icon and title. It visually tags content as machine-generated, which is an honesty and UX choice for an AI mail client. `?trailing` is Dart's null-aware collection element: the trailing widget is inserted only when it is non-null. The close button is optional via `onClose`.

lib/state/app_state.dart.overview: `AppState` is the central `ChangeNotifier` and the hub of the dependency graph. It owns every connected account session, the current view and selection, message actions, sending (undo, scheduling, follow-ups), local organization rules (snooze, VIP, block, mute), AI setup, background inbox triage, semantic indexing and the three-tier search. UI widgets watch it and call its methods, and it orchestrates `MailService`, `EmailAi`/`OllamaProvider`, `TriageCache`, `UserData` and `VectorIndex`. Most later tour steps (3, 8, 9, 12, 13) point back to a region of this file.

sections.title: Imports and view/session types
sections.explanation: `ViewKind` plus `MailView`'s const named constructors give cheap, comparable value objects for "what is the list showing", with `==`/`hashCode` overridden so views can be compared and used as keys. `isInboxBased` marks views derived from every account's inbox. `Toast` is a UI-agnostic message with an optional action. `OutgoingMail` captures everything needed to send or reopen a message (used for undo and failure recovery). `AccountSession` is the mutable per-account bag: connection, mailboxes, paged inbox, triage cache, and a vector index with its own separate `indexService` connection.

sections.title: AppState core and AI model selection
sections.explanation: Settings and accounts load synchronously from the store in the constructor. Toasts and undone sends are exposed as broadcast `Stream`s, so one-off events do not live in state, but events emitted when no widget is listening are dropped. `refreshAi` rebuilds the `OllamaProvider`, lists models and repairs settings that point to uninstalled models. `_pickDefault` parses parameter counts like `12b` from model names and prefers the one closest to 12B. `embeddingModel`/`translationModel` resolve to installed models or `''`. `updateSettings` clears and reindexes all vectors when the effective embedding model changes, because vectors from different models cannot be compared.

sections.title: Accounts: connect, add, remove
sections.explanation: Messages from enough_mail are not wrapped. Instead, two `Expando`s attach the owning session and mailbox to each `MimeMessage` (`_tag`), so any message in any list can find its account and folder. `init` loads `UserData`, discovers AI, starts a 30 s tick timer, connects all accounts in parallel, then starts a 3-minute refresh, auto-sort and indexing in the background. `_connect` turns credentials into a `MailService`, opens the triage cache, picks the inbox and records failures as friendly strings instead of throwing. `removeAccount` deletes keychain secrets (`deletePassword` removes both password and OAuth token), the triage cache and the vector file, then resets any view or selection pointing at that account.

sections.title: Views, filtering, paging and refresh
sections.explanation: `allInboxMessages` merges every account's inbox newest-first and memoizes it in `_mergedCache`. Every mutation must reset that cache to null, which the code does in many places and which is easy to forget when adding features. `_sortDate` makes a due snooze sort as if it just arrived. `_hiddenFromInbox` hides snoozed, blocked and muted mail. `_viewMessages` derives Priority/Needs reply/Category/VIP views from triage verdicts. Paging assumes 40 messages per page (`>= 40` means "has more") and de-duplicates by UID. `refresh` fetches the newest page, prepends unseen UIDs, and in quiet mode also retries failed accounts. `openFolder` and `loadMore` guard against races with `if (folderBox != box) return` after awaits.

sections.title: Opening messages and actions
sections.explanation: `openMessage` selects first (instant UI), then downloads the full body only if needed and swaps the full message into every list via `_replaceMessage`, re-tagging it with the Expandos. It then marks the message seen. Every action goes through `_act`, which runs the server operation, removes the message locally if it moved, and auto-selects the next message at the same index, which gives Apple-Mail-like keyboard triage. Errors become toasts, and the list is not updated optimistically, so the UI changes only after the server confirms.

sections.title: Sending, scheduling and the tick loop
sections.explanation: `sendMail` delays delivery by `undoSendSeconds` using a `Timer` per pending message. Undo cancels it and emits on `undoneSends` so the composer can reopen. **Risk:** pending sends exist only in memory, and `dispose` cancels them, so quitting during the undo window drops the message silently. Scheduled mail copies attachments into an app-support outbox and is persisted in `UserData`. It is sent by `_tick` only while the app is running, which the UI states. `_sendScheduled` removes the item before sending to avoid double sends and re-adds it on failure. A crash mid-send can still lose it. `_afterSent` learns contacts and records follow-ups, which `_tick` clears when a reply's `In-Reply-To`/`References` mentions the Message-ID.

sections.title: Organizing: snooze, VIP, block, mute, unsubscribe, files
sections.explanation: All of these rules live locally in `UserData`, not on the IMAP server. `snooze` keys reminders by `MailService.keyOf`. `_bringBack` re-fetches the message by UID if needed, marks it unread and shows a toast. `_remindedKeys` is in memory and due snoozes are not removed by `_tick`, so after a restart a due reminder can fire its toast again. `_applyRules` moves blocked senders' mail to Junk and archives muted threads (unless flagged) after every fetch, and swallows errors so the next fetch retries. `unsubscribe` tries RFC 8058 one-click POST, then mailto, then opening the web page. The POST has no timeout. Attachment saving sanitizes filenames and avoids overwriting with ` (n)` suffixes.

sections.title: Semantic indexing
sections.explanation: `indexAll` is single-flight: a call while one is running sets `_indexAgain` and reruns once afterwards. `_indexAccount` uses a separate `indexService` IMAP connection so background indexing does not block the UI connection. It walks the search folder (and Sent, except on Gmail) in pages of 100 headers, fetches full text only for unindexed UIDs (in batches of 25), and stops after 3 fully-known pages. `_indexMessages` embeds 16 at a time. `_semanticSearch` embeds the query with the model's prefix, searches each account's `VectorIndex` (minScore 0.25), groups hits by folder to fetch them back by UID, and evicts entries whose mail no longer exists. `_lastScores` is a shared field, so overlapping searches can overwrite each other's scores.

sections.title: Background AI triage
sections.explanation: `sortInboxes` collects inbox messages that are not in each account's `TriageCache`, sorts them newest-first so the visible mail is classified first, and sends them to `EmailAi.triage` in batches of 10. Progress (`sortDone/sortTotal`) is published after each batch. Like indexing, it is single-flight with a `_resortRequested` rerun flag, and `force` clears the caches for a full re-sort. AI failures stop the run with a toast and leave the partial results cached.

sections.title: Search, errors, test hooks and dispose
sections.explanation: `search` saves the previous view to restore later and scopes to the open folder or every account's search folder. It starts semantic search in parallel. Keyword mode runs IMAP search, then appends up to 10 semantic "related" hits scoring at least 0.4. AI mode has `EmailAi.planSearch` produce a `SearchPlan`, widens it if keywords found nothing, fuses IMAP and semantic lists with reciprocal rank fusion (`1/(60+rank)`), and has the model rank the top 30. `friendlyError` maps raw IMAP/OAuth/socket errors to plain advice by substring matching. `debugLoad` (`@visibleForTesting`) injects sample data for widget tests and screenshots. `dispose` cancels timers and pending sends, saves vectors and disconnects, but does not await these futures.

lib/ui/compose_page.dart.overview: ComposePage is the single editor screen for every kind of outgoing mail: new messages, replies and reply-all, forwards (with the original attachments), follow-up nudges, and restoring a message after Undo send or a failed send. It keeps its own form state in TextEditingControllers, but delegates sending, drafts, signatures, contacts and templates to AppState and UserData, and streams AI output from EmailAi straight into the body field. It is the main UI consumer of the writing half of the AI layer (Step 5) and the producer of OutgoingMail objects that AppState sends (Step 12).

sections.title: Constructor modes
sections.explanation: The widget's optional parameters double as its *mode*: `replyTo`, `forwardOf`, `restore` and `followUpOf` are mutually exclusive in practice, while `aiReplyInstruction` and `initialBody` modify a mode. Note the doc comment on `aiReplyInstruction`: a non-null but empty string still triggers an AI draft, so `null` vs `''` is meaningful. Importing `pickDateTime` from message_view.dart with `show` couples two screens; it works but suggests the helper could live in a shared widgets file.

sections.title: Form state fields
sections.explanation: All editor state lives here: one controller per field, a per-recipient-field `FocusNode` map for autocomplete, and flags for preview, Cc visibility, AI writer and attachment loading. `_generating` is derived from whether an AI stream subscription exists, so there is no separate boolean to keep in sync. `_initialSnapshot` is `late final` because it can only be taken after `initState` has filled the fields.

sections.title: initState: prefill per mode
sections.explanation: This block decides the sending account (restore, then the account that received the original, then the default) and prefills fields for each mode. Reply-all removes your own address and the reply-to targets from Cc; `Re:`/`Fwd:` prefixes are only added when missing. AI work (follow-up draft, AI reply) is deferred with `addPostFrameCallback` because `_runAi` calls `setState`, which is not allowed during `initState`. The `_dirty` getter compares a NUL-joined snapshot so the leave-confirmation only fires after real edits. Gotcha: `initialBody` is applied after a `restore`, so passing both would overwrite the restored body, and the snapshot is taken before forwarded attachments finish loading, so a forward counts as dirty as soon as they arrive.

sections.title: Reply language and forwarded files
sections.explanation: `_detectReplyLanguage` asks EmailAi (offline guess first, model second) what language the original is in, and only offers a translate-on-reply chip when it differs from the user's language setting. `_loadForwardedAttachments` downloads the original's attachments to local files through AppState and shows a loading chip meanwhile; both check `mounted` after the await, the standard guard against using a disposed State. `dispose` cancels any running AI stream and frees every controller and focus node.

sections.title: Streaming AI into the body
sections.explanation: `_runAi` is the shared engine for every AI writing tool: it saves the current text for Undo AI, clears the body, and appends each streamed chunk so the user watches the draft appear. When the stream finishes, `EmailAi.cleanDraft` strips code fences, preambles and stray Subject lines that small models add; on error the previous text is restored. `_stopAi` cancels mid-stream and keeps what was written so far. The body field is set `readOnly` while generating (see build), which prevents user edits from being overwritten by the next chunk.

sections.title: Building and sending mail
sections.explanation: `_finalBody` appends the per-account signature (using the standard `-- ` delimiter, and skipping it if already present), then either a forwarded-message block or a `>`-quoted original, so quoting happens in plain text before Markdown-to-HTML conversion in MailService. `_validate` parses all address fields up front so bad input fails in the UI rather than at SMTP time. `_send` confirms an empty subject, refuses immediate sends from a disconnected account (scheduled sends are allowed), then hands an `OutgoingMail` to `AppState.sendMail`, which owns the undo-send delay. `_sendLater` offers preset times plus a custom picker; as its own help text says, scheduling only works while the app is running. Risk: the Cmd+Enter shortcut calls `_send` directly, bypassing the disabled state the Send button has while AI is generating or attachments are loading.

sections.title: Leaving, drafts and templates
sections.explanation: `_confirmLeave` offers Discard, Keep editing or Save draft, and only allows leaving if the draft save succeeded, so a network failure never silently loses work. Templates use a heterogeneous dialog result (`Object`): a `Template` inserts its body, a Dart record `('delete', t)` removes it, and the string `'save'` stores the current body. This pattern-by-type approach avoids defining a result enum but means the dialog contract is only enforced at runtime.

sections.title: build: scaffold and fields
sections.explanation: `PopScope(canPop: !_dirty)` intercepts back navigation only when there are unsaved changes and routes it through `_confirmLeave`. The app bar holds attach, templates, Markdown preview, a follow-up reminder menu and a split Send / Send later button, both disabled while generating or loading attachments. The preview renders the body with `markdown`'s GitHub extension set through `HtmlWidget`, mirroring how MailService sends Markdown as HTML. The footer reveals behaviour that happens at send time (signature, quoted original, follow-up reminder) so it is not a surprise.

sections.title: From picker and recipient autocomplete
sections.explanation: The From dropdown appears only with multiple accounts and flags disconnected ones. `_recipientField` wraps `RawAutocomplete` around the shared controller: suggestions come from `UserData.suggestContacts` for the token after the last comma or semicolon, and selection rebuilds the field with a properly formatted `Name <email>` (quoting names containing commas). The `?trailing` syntax is Dart's null-aware collection element: it adds the widget only when it is non-null.

sections.title: AI toolbar and writer
sections.explanation: The toolbar shows a progress row with Stop while generating, otherwise chips: Write for me, one chip per `RewriteStyle`, a one-tap translate into the detected reply language, a translate menu and Undo AI. Translations here pass `forSending: true` so EmailAi uses the writing model, which produces more natural foreign text. `_aiWriter` is a prompt box that composes from notes when the body is empty or applies a free-form `customEdit` when there is text. Note that the email body and user prompts are sent verbatim to the model; that is fine locally, but malicious content in a quoted email can still steer the output, so users should read AI drafts before sending.

lib/services/ai/email_ai.dart.overview: EmailAi is the feature layer of the local AI stack: every assistant capability (summaries, Catch me up digests, quick replies, reply drafting, composing, rewriting, subject suggestions, triage, search planning and ranking, Q&A, translation and event extraction) is a prompt plus model choice on top of an abstract AiProvider. It depends only on the plain models from Step 4 and has no Flutter imports, so it can run from tests and command-line tools. Step 5 presents it as the top of the three AI tiers; the UI screens and AppState call into it.

sections.title: RewriteStyle enum
sections.explanation: An enhanced enum where each value carries a UI label and the exact instruction sent to the model. Keeping label and prompt together means adding a style automatically adds a chip in ComposePage, which iterates `RewriteStyle.values`.

sections.title: Configuration and writer rules
sections.explanation: The constructor takes two main models: a fast one for structured jobs and a writing model for text the user may send, plus optional translation and embedding models. An injectable `clock` makes date-dependent prompts deterministic in tests. `_writerRules` is a shared system prompt built with collection-if, enforcing body-only output, no invented facts (use `[placeholder]` instead), a sign-off with the user's first name and the user's personal style notes. Centralizing these rules keeps compose, draft-reply and similar features consistent.

sections.title: Reading: summary and digest
sections.explanation: `summarize` streams a fixed Markdown template (TL;DR, action items, key dates) from the fast model at low temperature for accuracy. `digest` powers Catch me up: it builds a numbered list of emails with trimmed bodies (skipping the first four header lines of `forPrompt`) and asks the writing model to group them into attention buckets. The `skip(4)` silently depends on the exact header layout of `EmailContent.forPrompt`; if that format changes, the digest input breaks quietly.

sections.title: Replying and writing
sections.explanation: `quickReplies` uses `completeJson` with a JSON schema so the model must return `{replies: [...]}`, and the result is defensively filtered and capped at three. `draftReply`, `compose`, `rewrite` and `customEdit` all return `Stream<String>` so ComposePage can show tokens live; grammar fixes use a very low temperature to discourage creative changes. `suggestSubject` post-processes the reply to strip a `Subject:` prefix and quotes, a common pattern when small models ignore formatting instructions. Email text goes into prompts verbatim, so a hostile email could attempt prompt injection; the output is only ever a suggestion the user reviews.

sections.title: Triage
sections.explanation: Triage sends a batch of compact email previews and a schema whose `category` and `priority` enums are generated from the `MailCategory` and `MailPriority` Dart enums, so the prompt and the model stay in sync. Results are matched back by index, and every index is bounds-checked before use because model output is untrusted. The prompt carefully defines high priority, needs_reply and suspicious (phishing), which feeds the smart inbox and phishing banners.

sections.title: Search: plan, rank, answer
sections.explanation: `planSearch` turns a natural-language query into a `SearchPlan` (keywords, sender, date range, flags), injecting today's date and weekday so relative ranges like 'last week' can be resolved. `rankResults` asks the model to reorder candidates and drops duplicates and out-of-range indexes with a `seen` set. `answerFromEmails` is a small retrieval-augmented Q&A: found emails become the context, and the prompt tells the model to cite the sender/subject and admit when the answer is missing.

sections.title: Translation
sections.explanation: `detectLanguage` tries the free offline `Languages.guess` first and only calls the model when unsure, swallowing errors to return null. `translate` is an `async*` generator that truncates very long input, picks the dedicated translation model for reading but the writing model when `forSending`, and switches to TranslateGemma's exact training prompt when that model is used, a detail backed by the project's model benchmark.

sections.title: Calendar extraction and cleanup
sections.explanation: `extractEvent` asks for a single event with ISO dates, then validates: `found` must be true, `start` must parse, and an `end` before `start` is discarded. `cleanDraft` is a static post-processor used by ComposePage to remove code fences, 'Here is...' preambles and a leading Subject line. The date helpers build `YYYY-MM-DD` manually instead of pulling in `intl`, keeping this file dependency-light.

sections.title: EmailEvent and .ics export
sections.explanation: `EmailEvent` is a small value class whose `toIcs` writes an RFC 5545 calendar file with CRLF line endings and escaped text. Missing ends default to one hour (or one day for all-day events). Times are written without a `TZID` or `Z`, i.e. as floating local times, which matches how the model was told to report them but means the event is interpreted in whatever time zone the calendar app uses. The UID is a timestamp, unique enough for one-off imports.

sections.title: Languages helper
sections.explanation: `Languages` provides picker names, ISO codes for the TranslateGemma prompt and a fast heuristic `guess`: first by Unicode script ranges (with Han resolved to Japanese if kana appear, and Cyrillic/Arabic left undecided because many languages share them), then by stop-word counts for Latin-script languages, returning only a clear winner. Risk: `code` falls back to `substring(0, 2)`, which throws a RangeError for a one-letter language name; names in normal use are safe.

lib/services/email_html.dart.overview: EmailHtml (the `EmailDocument` class) converts untrusted email bodies into safe, self-contained HTML pages for the reading pane. For HTML mail it sanitizes the DOM, blocks remote content and tracking pixels unless allowed, embeds `cid:` inline images, folds quoted history and injects a strict, nonce-based Content-Security-Policy. For plain-text mail it escapes, linkifies, nests quotes and dims signatures. Step 11 describes it as the first half of safe rendering; EmailWebView displays its output.

sections.title: EmailDocument and the CSP
sections.explanation: The class doc lists the security goals. `_nonce` uses `Random.secure()` for a fresh value per document, and `_csp` builds a policy that defaults to `'none'` and only lets the script carrying that nonce run. Remote images, styles and fonts are allowed only when `allowRemote` is true; frames, forms and `<base>` are always forbidden. This is defense in depth: even if sanitizing misses something, the CSP stops it from executing or phoning home.

sections.title: Stylesheets
sections.explanation: Three CSS blocks: a base style that makes mail readable and images responsive and styles the folded-quote `•••` summary; a plain-text style for wrapped text, quotes and signatures; and a dark palette applied only to plain-text mail. HTML emails always render on a light page (`color-scheme: light`) because senders design them for white backgrounds.

sections.title: Fit-to-width script
sections.explanation: The only script allowed to run, tagged with the nonce. It sets CSS `zoom` on the body when content is wider than the viewport, with a 0.35 lower bound, and re-runs on load, resize, DOMContentLoaded and two timeouts to catch late-loading images. This is why EmailWebView must enable JavaScript.

sections.title: fromHtml: sanitize and block
sections.explanation: Dangerous elements (scripts, frames, objects, `<base>`, `meta http-equiv`, HTML imports) are removed, then every `on*` event attribute and `javascript:` hrefs are stripped. `cid:` images are replaced with data URIs from the message. Blocked remote images become a transparent GIF with their aspect ratio preserved, while 1-2 px images (typical tracking pixels) are removed entirely. Note the sanitizer is a deny-list: `javascript:` is only checked on `href` and `[background]` attributes are counted but left in place, so the CSP is what actually prevents those from loading or running.

sections.title: fromHtml: assemble the page
sections.explanation: After folding quotes, our own `<meta>` tags (charset, CSP, viewport, color-scheme) and base CSS are inserted at the very start of `<head>`, creating a head if the email lacks one, so the CSP applies before any email content is parsed. The fit script is appended to the body and the result is returned with the blocked-image count, which the UI uses for its 'Load images' banner.

sections.title: fromPlain and linkify
sections.explanation: Plain-text mail gets a fully synthesized page with the same CSP, optional dark styles and the fit script. `_linkify` runs on already-escaped text and turns URLs, `www.` hosts and bare email addresses into links, excluding trailing punctuation from URLs. Escaping first and linkifying second is the safe order: no raw user text can become markup.

sections.title: plainToHtml: quotes and signature
sections.explanation: A two-pass algorithm. The first pass finds where quoted history starts, either a `>` line or a localized attribution ('On ... wrote:', German, French, Spanish, Outlook headers), but only if at least 60% of the remaining non-empty lines are quoted, avoiding folding inline replies. The second pass escapes each line, converts `>` depth into nested `<blockquote>`s, opens a `<details>` fold at the quote start and wraps everything after the `-- ` delimiter in a dimmed signature span. It is a static public method so the test suite can check it directly.

sections.title: Folding HTML quotes
sections.explanation: `_foldQuotes` recognizes quote containers from Gmail, Apple Mail, Yahoo and Outlook and wraps each (if it has meaningful text and is not already inside a fold) in a `<details class="lm-quote">`. For Outlook's `divRplyFwdMsg`/`appendonsend`, the header sits before the quoted body, so everything from that node to the end of its parent is moved into the fold. The private `nextNode` extension fills a gap in the `html` package's DOM API.

tool/screenshots_test.dart.overview: A widget-test file used as a developer tool: it renders the real app screens with sample mailboxes and a canned AI provider and saves PNGs into `screenshots/`, so documentation images can be regenerated without a mail account or Ollama. It also works as a high-level smoke test, since several tests assert on UI behavior. Step 15 lists it among the developer tools; it relies on AppState's `debugLoad` hook and on the AiProvider abstraction from Step 5.

sections.title: Header and imports
sections.explanation: The comments explain the purpose and run command (`flutter test tool/screenshots_test.dart`). The `ignore_for_file` silences warnings because the file calls `@visibleForTesting` members such as `debugLoad`. Living in `tool/` rather than `test/` keeps it out of the normal `flutter test` run, since it writes files and needs local font assets.

sections.title: CannedAi provider
sections.explanation: A fake `AiProvider` that returns fixed output: a quick-replies JSON when the system prompt asks for three suggestions and a JSON schema is given, otherwise a summary. It demonstrates the payoff of the provider abstraction: EmailAi runs unchanged on top of a fake. The detection by prompt substring is brittle; if the quick-reply prompt wording in EmailAi changes, the screenshot will quietly show a summary instead.

sections.title: Sample messages and fonts
sections.explanation: `mail()` builds real MIME messages with enough_mail's `MessageBuilder` and re-parses them, so the UI sees the same objects it would get from IMAP; UIDs count down to give a stable order. `loadFonts` loads Roboto and Material Icons from the Flutter SDK cache, because widget tests otherwise render text as boxes; the Homebrew fallback path ties it to macOS when `FLUTTER_ROOT` is unset. `snap` captures the `RepaintBoundary` at 1.5x inside `runAsync`, which is needed because image encoding is real async work outside the fake test clock.

sections.title: Sample app state
sections.explanation: `sampleState` mocks SharedPreferences, creates a real AppState and injects three accounts (Gmail, Microsoft and a side Gmail) with mailboxes, messages and precomputed triage via `debugLoad`, plus an EmailAi on top of CannedAi. `app()` wraps either the full `HearthmailApp` or a single page in a themed MaterialApp, inside the RepaintBoundary that `snap` captures. Note `now` is a top-level final, so relative dates are fixed when the file loads.

sections.title: Screenshot tests
sections.explanation: Each `testWidgets` sets a window size, builds the state, drives the UI (tapping Summarize and Quick replies, right-clicking with `kSecondaryButton`, switching to dark mode) and saves a numbered PNG. The context-menu test also asserts that the menu items exist and that 'Add sender to VIPs' updates UserData, so it doubles as a behavior test. The dark-mode test clears the brightness override only at the end, so a failure before that line could leak dark mode into later tests.

lib/ui/home_page.dart.overview: HomePage is the app shell shown after setup: a responsive layout with sidebar, message list and reading pane side by side on wide windows, and a single pane with a drawer on phones. It listens to AppState's toast and undone-send streams, binds Apple-Mail-style keyboard shortcuts and hosts the AI 'Catch me up' digest dialog. Step 10 introduces it as the frame that MessageView and the AI widgets live in.

sections.title: Imports and widget
sections.explanation: HomePage is a StatefulWidget because it owns a search FocusNode (shared with the list pane for Cmd+F), two stream subscriptions and the phone-only flag `_showingMessageOnPhone`. The doc comment states the key design choice: one code path serves desktop, tablet and phone by switching layout on width.

sections.title: Toast and undo-send streams
sections.explanation: In `initState` the page subscribes to `AppState.toasts` to show SnackBars and to `undoneSends` to reopen a ComposePage with the cancelled or failed message. Using streams rather than callbacks keeps AppState free of BuildContext, and the `mounted` checks avoid touching a disposed widget. `context.read` (not `watch`) is correct here because initState must not register a rebuild dependency. Subscriptions and the FocusNode are released in `dispose`.

sections.title: Navigation and Catch me up
sections.explanation: `_compose` and `_settings` push full-screen routes. `_catchUp` picks up to 30 unread inbox messages, falling back to the latest 20 when fewer than three are unread, and opens a dialog whose `AiStreamView` streams `EmailAi.digest` token by token inside an `AiCard` that labels the content as AI-generated. The `start` callback form lets the view start (and restart) the stream itself.

sections.title: Keyboard shortcuts
sections.explanation: Shortcuts are a map from `SingleActivator` to callbacks, consumed by `CallbackShortcuts`; message actions are added with a collection-if spread only when a message is selected. They mirror Apple Mail (Cmd+R reply, Cmd+Shift+R reply all, Cmd+Backspace delete and so on). All use `meta: true`, so on Windows and Linux they need the Windows/Super key rather than Ctrl, a likely gap if desktop support beyond macOS matters.

sections.title: Responsive layout and scaffold
sections.explanation: The app bar shows Catch me up only when AI is ready and the inbox is not empty, as a labelled button on wide screens and an icon on narrow ones. At 900 px or wider the body is a Row of fixed-width sidebar (240) and list (380) plus an expanded MessageView; on phones it toggles between the list and the message with a back callback, and the sidebar moves into a Drawer. `Focus(autofocus: true)` gives the shortcut tree keyboard focus on launch.

test/features_test.dart.overview: The main unit-test suite for pure logic. It covers HTML sanitization and plain-text rendering in EmailDocument, offline language detection, the vector index and embedding prompt formats, MailService header helpers (unsubscribe, phishing hints, threading), .ics export and UserData contacts and blocking. None of it needs a network, mail server or Ollama, which is the testing strategy Step 15 describes.

sections.title: Imports and MIME helper
sections.explanation: `msg()` builds a real `MimeMessage` from header text with enough_mail's parser, so header helpers are tested against the same type they process in production, without a server.

sections.title: EmailDocument tests
sections.explanation: These tests pin down the security contract from Step 11: scripts, `onload`, `javascript:` links and remote images are gone, the tracking pixel is removed, the hero image is blocked but counted, `cid:` images are inlined and the CSP contains a nonce and a restrictive `img-src`. Further tests check that `allowRemote` relaxes the CSP, that Gmail quotes fold, that plain text gets links, nested quotes, a dimmed signature and correct HTML escaping. Exact string assertions like `"img-src data: cid:;"` are strict, so harmless reformatting of the CSP will also break them.

sections.title: Language and vector tests
sections.explanation: `Languages.guess` is checked on English, German, French, Hindi and Japanese samples and must stay silent on very short text. The VectorIndex test verifies nearest-neighbor ordering with a minimum score and removal, and the embedding tests confirm that each embedding model gets the prompt prefix format it was trained with.

sections.title: MailService helper tests
sections.explanation: Covers parsing `List-Unsubscribe` (mailto and web, plus one-click), the phishing heuristic (a brand name or address in the display name that does not match the real domain is suspicious, genuine senders are not) and conversation grouping via Message-ID, In-Reply-To and References, including subject normalization across Re/AW/Fwd prefixes.

sections.title: Calendar and contacts tests
sections.explanation: The .ics test checks the default one-hour end, comma escaping and all-day next-day ends. The UserData test confirms contact suggestions rank by weight, match on name too, hide no-reply addresses, and that domain blocks such as `@spam.biz` match case-insensitively.

pubspec.yaml.overview: The Dart/Flutter package manifest: it names the app, pins the SDK and lists the dependencies that the rest of the tour builds on. Step 2 uses it to introduce the building blocks: enough_mail for IMAP/SMTP, http for Ollama and OAuth, flutter_secure_storage for secrets, webview_flutter for rendering mail and provider for state. Most of the file is unchanged `flutter create` boilerplate comments.

sections.title: Package identity and SDK
sections.explanation: `publish_to: 'none'` keeps this private app off pub.dev. `version: 1.0.0+1` is the user-facing version plus build number used by each platform. The description is still the template's 'A new Flutter project.', a small leftover worth updating. `sdk: ^3.14.0` requires Dart 3.14 or newer below 4.0, which the code relies on for features like records, patterns and null-aware collection elements (`?trailing`).

sections.title: Runtime dependencies
sections.explanation: Each package maps to a layer: `enough_mail` (IMAP/SMTP and MIME), `http` (Ollama and OAuth), `provider` (AppState), `shared_preferences` and `flutter_secure_storage` (settings vs Keychain secrets), `path_provider`, `html` and `markdown` (sanitizing, plain text and sending Markdown as HTML), `webview_flutter` and `flutter_widget_from_html_core` (main and fallback mail rendering), `url_launcher`, `intl`, `crypto` (PKCE hashing) and `file_selector` (attachments). `material_ui` supplies the Material widgets imported throughout the UI. Caret constraints allow compatible minor updates.

sections.title: Dev dependencies
sections.explanation: Only `flutter_test` and `flutter_lints` are needed, consistent with tests that use fakes and in-memory stores instead of mocking frameworks.

sections.title: Flutter section
sections.explanation: `uses-material-design: true` bundles the Material Icons font. Everything else is commented template guidance; the app ships no custom assets or fonts.

lib/ui/email_web_view.dart.overview: EmailWebView displays the safe page produced by EmailDocument in the platform web engine (WebKit or Chromium) through webview_flutter, and opens any link the user clicks in the external browser instead of navigating inside the app. Where no web view exists (Windows, the web, tests) it falls back to the pure-Flutter HtmlWidget renderer. It is the second half of Step 11's safe rendering pipeline.

sections.title: Widget and platform support
sections.explanation: `supported` checks for macOS, iOS or Android and a registered `WebViewPlatform`; the `!kIsWeb` check comes first because `dart:io`'s `Platform` throws on the web. Checking `WebViewPlatform.instance` also makes widget tests fall back automatically, since no plugin is registered there.

sections.title: Controller and navigation policy
sections.explanation: JavaScript is enabled only so the nonce-tagged fit-to-width script can run; the email's own scripts are still blocked by the CSP set by EmailDocument. The navigation delegate allows only `about:` and `data:` loads (the initial HTML) and prevents everything else, launching main-frame link targets externally. Risk: any parsable scheme is handed to `launchUrl`, so links such as `file:` or custom app schemes in a malicious email would be passed to the OS; an allowlist of `http`, `https` and `mailto` would be tighter. Setting the background is wrapped in try/catch because some platforms do not implement it.

sections.title: Loading and updates
sections.explanation: `_load` remembers the last HTML string and skips reloads when it has not changed, so rebuilds of the parent do not flash the web view. `didUpdateWidget` reloads when a new message (or an allow-images variant) arrives. A changed `background` is not reapplied after init, which matters only if the theme changes while a message is open.

sections.title: Build and fallback renderer
sections.explanation: With a controller the widget is simply `WebViewWidget`. Otherwise `HtmlWidget` renders the same HTML in a scroll view with text color chosen from the background's luminance and taps opening externally. The fallback does not execute scripts or enforce the CSP, but since EmailDocument already removed scripts and blocked remote images in the markup, it stays reasonably safe.

lib/services/html_text.dart.overview: Two small HTML utilities used outside the reading pane. `htmlToText` turns an HTML email into readable plain text for AI prompts and list previews, and `blockRemoteImages` strips remote images from HTML. Step 6 lists it beside MailService because MailService uses it to extract AI-ready body text; Step 11 groups it with the HTML safety code.

sections.title: Block tag set
sections.explanation: The set of tags after which a newline is written, so paragraphs, list items, table rows and headings keep their visual separation in the text output.

sections.title: htmlToText
sections.explanation: Parses with the `html` package, removes non-content elements (scripts, styles, head, title, noscript) and walks the DOM recursively, collapsing whitespace in text nodes, prefixing list items with `- ` and appending link targets in parentheses when they are http links not already visible and shorter than 120 characters, which gives the AI useful context without long tracking URLs. A final pass trims lines and limits blank lines to one. The fallback `doc.body ?? doc.documentElement ?? doc` handles fragments without a body.

sections.title: blockRemoteImages
sections.explanation: Removes `` elements whose `src` starts with `http` and returns the original string untouched if nothing was removed, avoiding a needless re-serialization. It is simpler than EmailDocument's handling: protocol-relative `//` URLs, `srcset`, CSS backgrounds and `` sources are not covered, so it should not be relied on as the primary anti-tracking defense; the CSP in EmailDocument does that job for displayed mail.

macos/Runner/DebugProfile.entitlements.overview: The App Sandbox entitlements for macOS Debug and Profile builds. Each key maps to a feature from earlier steps: outgoing network for IMAP/SMTP, OAuth and Ollama; an incoming network listener for the OAuth loopback redirect; and file access for attachments. Step 14 notes that the Release file is the same minus `allow-jit`.

sections.title: Sandbox and network
sections.explanation: `app-sandbox` confines the app; `network.client` permits outgoing connections to mail servers, OAuth endpoints and the local Ollama server; `network.server` allows listening on a localhost port, which the OAuth loopback redirect needs. `cs.allow-jit` is required only in debug and profile builds because the Dart VM JIT-compiles code there for hot reload; release builds are AOT-compiled and drop it.

sections.title: File access
sections.explanation: `files.user-selected.read-write` lets the app read files the user picks in the open panel (attachments) and write where they choose to save; `files.downloads.read-write` allows saving attachments directly into Downloads. These are the narrowest file entitlements that fit the features, consistent with the privacy-first design.

macos/Runner/Configs/AppInfo.xcconfig.overview: Xcode build settings that give the macOS app its identity: product name, bundle identifier and copyright, plus an optional include of a local signing config. Step 14 groups it with the entitlements and signing example as the platform configuration layer.

sections.title: App identity
sections.explanation: `PRODUCT_NAME` sets the app and window title, `PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER` (`app.hearthmail.hearthmail`) is how macOS identifies the app for the sandbox container and Keychain access, and the copyright appears in About. Changing the bundle ID would make existing Keychain items and sandbox data unreachable for the new identity.

sections.title: Optional signing include
sections.explanation: `#include?` with a question mark is an optional include: if `Signing.xcconfig` is absent (the default for a fresh checkout) the build still succeeds and is signed ad hoc. This lets each developer keep their own team ID in an untracked file.

macos/Runner/Configs/Signing.xcconfig.ex.overview: A template for the developer's local `Signing.xcconfig`, which AppInfo.xcconfig optionally includes. Signing with a stable Apple Development identity matters for Hearthmail because credentials live in the Keychain: with ad hoc signing, macOS sees each rebuild as a different app and asks for Keychain access again.

sections.title: Signing settings
sections.explanation: The comments explain the workflow: copy to `Signing.xcconfig`, insert your team ID from Xcode. `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM` and `CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY = Apple Development` give every local build the same signature, so Keychain access granted once stays granted. Keeping the real file out of version control avoids committing personal team IDs.

lib/ui/message_view.dart.overview: The reading pane: everything shown once an email is selected. It has the toolbar (reply, archive, flag, remind me, a More menu), the header with sender, recipients and status banners, the AI action bar (summarize, quick replies, add to calendar, translate, reply with AI), attachment chips and the sandboxed HTML body. It also exports helpers that other screens use: `openReply`, `openForward`, `snoozeChoices`, `pickDateTime` and the right-click `showMessageMenu` that `message_list.dart` imports. It is the main file of the 'App Shell and Reading Pane' tour step. Most actions are delegated to `AppState`, so this file stays mostly presentation and short-lived UI state.

sections.title: Imports and compose helpers
sections.explanation: Imports the enough_mail model, the AI service, the HTML pipeline (`email_html.dart`, `email_web_view.dart`) and `AppState`. `openReply` and `openForward` are top-level functions, not methods, so the toolbar, the context menu, the AI bar and the quick-reply buttons all open `ComposePage` the same way. The optional `aiInstruction` is how an AI draft request goes to the composer: this file only passes the instruction, and the composer does the generation.

sections.title: Snooze times and date picker
sections.explanation: `snoozeChoices` builds the Apple Mail and Gmail style 'Remind me' presets as `(label, DateTime)` records. The optional `from` argument makes it testable with a fixed clock. The modulo arithmetic finds the *next* Saturday and Monday; when today is already that day it adds 7 days instead of returning today. 'This evening' only appears before 17:00 and 'This weekend' only Monday to Thursday. `pickDateTime` chains a date picker and a time picker. It checks `context.mounted` between the two awaits, which is the usual guard against using a disposed context after an async gap.

sections.title: MessageView: empty state and keying
sections.explanation: The top-level pane watches `AppState` and shows a placeholder when nothing is selected. The important detail is `_MessageBody(key: ObjectKey(m))`. Because the key is the message object, selecting another email creates a fresh `State`. Translation, summaries, quick replies and the parsed-document cache are then reset instead of leaking from the previous email. The other half of that design: an in-place update that replaces the `MimeMessage` instance (a reload, for example) also discards that UI state.

sections.title: MessageToolbar actions
sections.explanation: The toolbar uses `context.read` (not `watch`), because the parent `MessageView` already rebuilds on state changes. Under 700 px wide (`narrow`) it moves Reply all and Forward into the More menu. Local closures (`snoozeMenu`, `moveMenu`, `confirmBlock`) keep the dialog logic next to the buttons. The `Builder` around the alarm button gets a `BuildContext` for that button, so the snooze menu opens under it. The tooltips list Apple Mail shortcuts (⌘R, ⌘E, ⇧⌘L), but the shortcuts are bound elsewhere. Note: the move and block dialogs are repeated almost line for line in `showMessageMenu` below, so a fix to one must be copied to the other.

sections.title: Body state, language detection, translation
sections.explanation: `_MessageBodyState` keeps the short-lived per-email UI state: summary/quick-reply toggles, remote-image opt-in, translation progress and busy flags. `initState` starts `_detectLanguage`, which asks the local AI for the email's language. The translate banner only appears when that language differs from the user's `myLanguage` setting. `_translate` streams chunks from `ai.translate` into a `StringBuffer` and keeps the `StreamSubscription` so `dispose` can cancel it. Every `setState` is guarded by `mounted`, which matters because the user can switch emails while a stream is still running.

sections.title: Calendar, unsubscribe and document cache
sections.explanation: `_addToCalendar` asks the AI to extract an event and then shows a confirmation dialog that says the details were 'Found by AI'. Calendar opens for a final check, so a model error does not silently create a wrong event. `_unsubscribe` confirms first and sends the result text (or a `friendlyError`) to a toast. `_document` caches the parsed `EmailDocument` under a string key made of image permission, theme, translation state and translated length, so HTML is not re-parsed on every rebuild. During streaming translation the length changes with every chunk, so the plain document is rebuilt once per chunk, which is intended. `_inline` resolves `cid:` images to base64 `data:` URIs, which can use a lot of memory for large inline images.

sections.title: Header and status banners
sections.explanation: `build` collects everything the header needs: suspicion (forged-sender check from `MailService.suspicionOf` first, then the AI triage flag), unsubscribe info, snooze, VIP status and attachments. A local `banner` helper draws the stacked notices (phishing warning, reminder, translation, mailing list, blocked remote images). The 'Load images' banner only appears when the HTML document reports `blockedImages > 0`, so plain emails never show it. Risks: `isHtml` decodes the HTML part again on every build, which partly undoes the cache. `MailService.senderName(m).characters.first` throws a `StateError` if the sender name is an empty string.

sections.title: Body layout and AI bar
sections.explanation: The `LayoutBuilder` limits the scrollable header to 55% of the pane height, so the email body always gets space. The body container stays white for HTML even in dark mode (as the comment explains, HTML email is designed for a white page) and only follows the theme for plain text. `_aiBar` creates the quick-replies `Future` once and stores it in state, so `FutureBuilder` does not restart the request on every rebuild. The 'Reply with AI' field passes the typed text to `openReply`. The suffix button does this even when the field is empty. Clicking a quick reply opens the composer with that short reply as the AI instruction.

sections.title: Attachment chips
sections.explanation: Each attachment is an `InputChip` with two actions: tap opens the file, and the 'delete' icon, reused as a download button, saves it to Downloads. Both call `AppState.saveAttachment`. A local `_busy` flag disables the chip and shows a spinner while it runs. Errors go through `AppState.friendlyError`, so the toast text stays readable. `_size` formats bytes as B, KB or MB.

sections.title: Right-click message menu
sections.explanation: `showMessageMenu` is the Apple Mail style context menu used by the message list (right-click on desktop, long-press on phones). The menu is placed with `RelativeRect.fromRect` against the overlay's size, so it opens at the pointer. After the menu returns it checks `context.mounted`, then switches on the chosen action; the 'remind' and 'move' cases open more dialogs. `sender!` is safe here because those items are only added when `sender != null`. The `EventFinder` typedef above is not used in this file; its comment says it is for the event dialog and tests.

lib/ui/message_list.dart.overview: The middle column of the app: the search bar, a title row for the current view, filter chips, and the scrolling message list with paging, swipe gestures and context menus. It also has the special lists for Scheduled and Follow-up views and the `MessageTile` row widget with its triage tags. It is where the 'Search: Keyword, AI and Semantic' tour step shows up in the UI: the search bar chooses between AI and keyword search, and `_SearchHeader` can stream an AI answer drawn from the top results. All data and actions come from `AppState` through Provider.

sections.title: Imports and relative dates
sections.explanation: The file imports `material_ui` rather than `package:flutter/material.dart`, presumably the project's Material re-export. It imports only `showMessageMenu` from `message_view.dart`, which keeps the coupling between the two panes small. `formatListDate` follows the usual mail-client pattern: time for today, weekday for the last 6 days, month and day for this year, and the full date for older mail. It always converts to local time first.

sections.title: Pane header, title and filters
sections.explanation: `MessageListPane` watches `AppState` and uses an exhaustive Dart 3 `switch` expression over `ViewKind` to pick the title. Adding a new view kind will fail to compile until it gets a title, which is useful. The 'Mark all as read' button only appears when some message is unread. The filter chips (All/Unread/Flagged/Attachments) are hidden for Search, Scheduled and Follow-up views, where they make no sense. The body chooses between the two special lists and the normal message list.

sections.title: Loading, error and empty states
sections.explanation: `_buildList` handles the non-happy paths in priority order. It shows a spinner while connecting with nothing to show yet, and a per-account error panel with a single 'Try again' button when *no* account is connected and some have failed. Then it shows a context-specific empty message (for example 'Sorting your inbox…' while AI triage runs for smart views). A partly failed setup, where one account works and another fails, still shows the list. The failure only becomes a full-screen error when nothing is connected.

sections.title: Paged list with swipe and menus
sections.explanation: Infinite scroll uses a `NotificationListener` that calls `state.loadMore()` within 400 px of the end, plus a spinner row at the end. This handler fires on every scroll notification, so `AppState.loadMore` must ignore repeated calls while a page is loading. Each row is wrapped in a `GestureDetector` for right-click and long-press menus. Below 700 px it is also wrapped in a `Dismissible` (right swipe archives, left swipe deletes). The `Dismissible` uses `ObjectKey(m)`, so the identity of the `MimeMessage` instance matters. The 'suspicious' tag combines the header-based forgery check with the AI triage flag.

sections.title: Search bar with AI toggle
sections.explanation: A stateful search field with a switch that chooses between AI search and plain keyword search. The switch is disabled when `state.aiReady` is false, and the effective value is `_useAi && state.aiReady`. Submitting calls `state.search(q, useAi: ai)`. The hint text changes to 'Ask anything…' in AI mode. A detail to notice: `build` clears the controller as a side effect when the app leaves search mode and the field is not focused. It works, but changing state during build can be surprising.

sections.title: Search status and AI answer
sections.explanation: `_SearchHeader` shows the search progress text. After an AI search finishes, it decides once per query (tracked in `_answeredFor`) whether the query looks like a question: it ends with '?' or starts with an interrogative matched by a regex. If so, it opens an 'Answer' card automatically. Otherwise an 'Ask AI' button lets the user request one. The answer streams from `ai.answerFromEmails` over the top 6 results. `ValueKey('answer:$q')` restarts the stream when the query changes.

sections.title: MessageTile row and tags
sections.explanation: `MessageTile` draws one row: an unread dot, a VIP star, the sender (bold when unread), flag and attachment icons, the date, the subject and a 2-line preview with whitespace collapsed. The tag row is only built when at least one tag applies. Tags include reminder, Suspicious, Priority, Needs reply (hidden once the message `isAnswered`), category (using `categoryColor` from the sidebar) and the account badge, added with Dart's null-aware element `?account`. `MailService.bodyText` runs on every build of every visible tile, which could be slow for large messages.

sections.title: Scheduled sends list
sections.explanation: The Scheduled view lists messages queued by this app's 'send later' feature (stored in `userData.scheduled`, so it is local to this computer, as FEATURES.md notes). Each row shows recipient, send time and sending account, with 'Send now' and 'Cancel' buttons that call `AppState`. The empty state tells the user where the feature is found in the composer.

sections.title: Follow-up reminders list
sections.explanation: The Follow-up view splits reminders into *due* (no reply yet, highlighted) and *waiting*, sorted by due date under a 'WAITING' label. A due item gets a 'Follow up' button that opens `ComposePage(followUpOf: f)`. Every item can be dismissed. The local `tile` closure avoids a separate widget class for this small list.

tool/model_bench.dart.overview: A command-line benchmark (`dart run tool/model_bench.dart embed|chat|translate`) that compares local Ollama models on the app's real jobs: semantic search retrieval, triage sorting accuracy and writing speed, and translation quality. Its results are the numbers quoted in FEATURES.md's 'Local AI: which model does what' table (for example 40/40 top-1 retrieval for embeddinggemma), which back the default model choices. It talks directly to Ollama's HTTP API and does not import any app code, so its prompts and JSON schema copy the app's instead of sharing them. It belongs to the 'Tests and Model Benchmarks' tour step.

sections.title: Usage header and constants
sections.explanation: The header comment documents the three modes and the requirement that Ollama is running. `avoid_print` is turned off for the file because console output is the whole point. `base` hard-codes Ollama's default `localhost:11434` endpoint.

sections.title: Synthetic email corpus
sections.explanation: Fifty `(subject, body)` records written to resemble a real student/worker inbox in Berlin: flights, invoices, course deadlines, German and French mail. From index 30 there are deliberate look-alike distractors (another Lisbon flight email, another invoice, another thesis email). Their job is to make retrieval hard enough to separate the models.

sections.title: Retrieval queries
sections.explanation: Forty `(query, expected email index)` pairs. The first 20 are direct, and the second 20 are paraphrases, cross-language queries ('Mieterhöhung', 'Hautarzt Termin') and short name-based queries ('Max Sony'). The ground truth is a single correct index per query, so the metrics below measure exact-document retrieval.

sections.title: HTTP and vector helpers
sections.explanation: `post` wraps Ollama JSON calls and throws on any non-200 response. `norm` truncates a vector to `dims` and L2-normalizes it, so dot product equals cosine similarity. This also lets the benchmark test Matryoshka-style truncated embeddings. `embed` calls `/api/embed` with a batch of inputs and `keep_alive` so the model stays loaded between calls.

sections.title: Embedding benchmark
sections.explanation: Each model gets its own query/document prompt templates (embeddinggemma's `task: search result | query:` format, and qwen3-embedding's instruction prefix), which affect retrieval quality. After a warm-up call it times batch document embedding and per-query embedding. It then ranks all documents for each query at the full size, 512 and 256 dimensions, and reports top-1, top-3 and MRR. The 512-dimension result explains the app's 512-number vectors described in FEATURES.md.

sections.title: Chat speed and sorting accuracy
sections.explanation: `labels` gives expected category and priority for 20 emails. `benchChat` first measures writing speed with Ollama's own `eval_count`/`eval_duration` counters (tokens per second) on a reply-to-Priya task. It then sorts in batches of 10, 'like the app', using a JSON-schema `format` with enum-constrained category and priority, plus a system prompt that defines 'high' priority. Out-of-range indexes are skipped, and parse failures are silently ignored by the empty `catch`, so a model that returns malformed JSON simply scores lower.

sections.title: Translation comparison
sections.explanation: Five samples (German, French, Hindi, Japanese, English) are translated into English, or into German for the English sample. translategemma models get their documented single-user-turn prompt template; other models get a generic translator system prompt. Output is printed for a person to judge; there is no automatic score. This is how FEATURES.md concludes that translategemma is most faithful for reading mail.

sections.title: Entry point
sections.explanation: `main` picks the mode (default `embed`) and accepts optional model names after it. Default model lists match those in FEATURES.md. An unknown mode does nothing and still exits 0. `exit(0)` forces the process to end even if HTTP connections are still open.

lib/services/oauth.dart.overview: Implements 'Sign in with Google / Microsoft' for IMAP/SMTP using OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow with PKCE and a temporary loopback HTTP server as redirect target. Users register their own OAuth app (see OAUTH_SETUP.md), so `OAuthClient` takes the client ID (and Google's optional secret) as input instead of hard-coding them. It returns an enough_mail `OauthToken` plus the email and name read from the ID token, and can refresh access tokens later. It is the core of the 'Sign-In: OAuth and Keychain' tour step; `settings_store.dart` persists what it returns.

sections.title: Imports and design note
sections.explanation: It uses `dart:io` `HttpServer` for the loopback redirect, `crypto` for the PKCE SHA-256 challenge, `http` for token calls and `url_launcher` to open the system browser. The doc comment summarizes the flow: the browser signs in and sends a one-time code to a server on 127.0.0.1 that runs for a few minutes.

sections.title: Constructors and injectable deps
sections.explanation: Two named constructors set the provider `kind`.
