Google normalizes an empty or whitespace-only secret to `null`, and Microsoft never has one (it is a public client). `http.Client` and `openBrowser` are optional injections. Production uses the global `http` functions and `launchUrl`; tests pass a `MockClient` and a fake browser. This keeps the class testable without a real browser or network.

sections.title: Provider endpoints, scopes, servers
sections.explanation: Per-provider endpoints and scopes are getters that switch on `_google`. Google uses the full `https://mail.google.com/` scope (required for IMAP/SMTP XOAUTH2). Microsoft asks for the Outlook IMAP and SMTP delegated scopes plus `offline_access` for a refresh token. `servers` returns a Dart record with the matching IMAP/SMTP hosts and ports (Gmail SMTP over SSL 465, Office 365 STARTTLS 587), so account setup can fill these in automatically.

sections.title: PKCE values and loopback servers
sections.explanation: `signIn` creates a 64-character PKCE verifier and its S256 challenge (base64url without padding), plus a random `state` against CSRF. It binds IPv4 loopback on port 0 (the OS picks a free port) and tries the same port on IPv6, since 'localhost' can resolve to `::1` in the browser. Any IPv6 failure is ignored. The redirect URI differs by provider: Google wants the `127.0.0.1` literal, and Microsoft registrations use `localhost`, as the comment notes.

sections.title: Redirect request handler
sections.explanation: A `Completer` connects the HTTP callback to the waiting `signIn`. Requests without `code` or `error` (such as a favicon fetch) get a 404 and are ignored. Otherwise it serves a small 'you can close this tab' page and completes with the query parameters. The first matching request wins, and the state is checked afterwards. So a stray local request with a wrong `state` ends the sign-in with an error rather than being skipped. That is safe, but any local process can make the attempt fail.

sections.title: Authorization URL and waiting
sections.explanation: It builds the authorization URL with collection-if/spread (Google: `access_type=offline`, `prompt=consent` to make sure a refresh token comes back; Microsoft: `select_account`). `'login_hint': ?loginHint` uses Dart's newer null-aware map entry syntax, which leaves the key out when the value is null. It opens the browser, waits up to 5 minutes, maps provider errors to friendly text, and rejects a `state` mismatch.

sections.title: Code exchange and identity
sections.explanation: Exchanges the code with the PKCE `code_verifier` (and the secret only if one exists). Microsoft also repeats `scope`. It refuses to continue without a refresh token, because the user would otherwise be signed out within an hour. The email comes from unverified ID-token claims (`email`, then `preferred_username`, then the login hint). That is acceptable here because the token came straight from the token endpoint over TLS. The `finally` block always cancels subscriptions and force-closes both servers, so ports are not left open after a failure or timeout.

sections.title: Token refresh and POST helper
sections.explanation: `refresh` sends a `refresh_token` grant. `_token`'s `fallbackRefresh` keeps the old refresh token when the provider does not rotate it (Google usually does not). `_post` applies a 30 s timeout and turns `SocketException` into 'No internet connection.' Risk: `jsonDecode(res.body)` runs before the status check, so a non-JSON error page (a proxy or captive portal, for example) throws a `FormatException` instead of an `OAuthException`. A `TimeoutException` is also not wrapped.

sections.title: Parsing, error mapping, randomness
sections.explanation: `_token` builds the enough_mail `OauthToken` with sensible defaults (3600 s, Bearer) and records `provider: kind.name`, which tells the app later which client should refresh it. `_idClaims` base64url-decodes the JWT payload without verifying the signature and returns `{}` on any problem. `_describeError` maps common failures, including Azure AD codes (AADSTS65001 admin consent, AADSTS700016 unknown app) and Google's `org_internal`, to advice for university users. `_randomString` uses `Random.secure()` over the RFC 7636 unreserved character set.

sections.title: Result and exception types
sections.explanation: `OAuthResult` bundles the token with the email and display name for account creation. `OAuthException.toString()` returns only the message, so the UI can show it directly to the user.

lib/services/settings_store.dart.overview: Defines `AppSettings`, the immutable app-wide preferences (Ollama URL and model choices, writing profile, privacy and search options, the user's own OAuth client IDs), and `SettingsStore`, which saves settings and account configs as JSON in SharedPreferences and keeps passwords and OAuth tokens in the OS keychain through flutter_secure_storage. It is the 'Keychain' half of the 'Sign-In: OAuth and Keychain' tour step and the storage behind the Settings page (tour step 13).

sections.title: AppSettings fields and defaults
sections.explanation: An immutable value class whose constructor defaults are the out-of-the-box configuration: local Ollama at `localhost:11434`, empty model names (meaning 'pick automatically'), auto-sort on, remote images *off* for privacy, semantic search on, 10 s undo-send, 3,000-email index depth. The comments separate `fastModel` (structured jobs) from `writingModel` (text you send), the split FEATURES.md justifies with benchmarks.

sections.title: copyWith
sections.explanation: The standard immutable-update pattern: every field is optional and falls back to the current value. One limitation of `??`: a field cannot be set back to `null` this way. That is not a problem here because every field is non-nullable.

sections.title: JSON serialization
sections.explanation: `toJson`/`fromJson` map fields one to one. Every read in `fromJson` has its own default, so a settings blob from an older version with missing keys still loads. Risk: the casts are strict (`as int?`, `as bool?`). A value of the wrong type throws, and `loadSettings` catches that by resetting *all* settings to defaults rather than only the bad field. Note also that `googleClientSecret` is written here into plain SharedPreferences, not the keychain. OAUTH_SETUP.md says that secret is not truly secret for desktop apps.

sections.title: Store setup and keychain options
sections.explanation: `SettingsStore` has a private constructor and an async `open()` factory, because `SharedPreferences.getInstance()` is async. The secure storage is configured with `usesDataProtectionKeychain: false`. The comment explains why: the classic login keychain works for unsigned local macOS builds, while the data-protection keychain needs a paid developer signature. Keys carry a `.v1` suffix, which leaves room for future format migrations.

sections.title: Settings and accounts persistence
sections.explanation: Loading is defensive: a missing or corrupt blob gives defaults or an empty account list instead of crashing at startup. The account configs themselves (servers, auth type, and so on) are stored as JSON in preferences. Only secrets go to the keychain.

sections.title: Passwords and OAuth tokens
sections.explanation: Secrets are stored per account under `password.<id>` and `oauth.<id>`. `deletePassword` removes *both* keys, so removing an account also deletes its OAuth token, as promised in OAUTH_SETUP.md's privacy section. `readToken` returns `null` on a corrupt token, which the app should treat as 'sign in again'.

test/oauth_test.dart.overview: Unit tests for `OAuthClient` that run the real loopback-server flow without a network. A fake browser reads the authorization URL and makes a real HTTP request back to the app's local server, and `MockClient` stands in for the token endpoint. The tests cover PKCE correctness, provider-specific parameters, CSRF state checking, error mapping and refresh-token retention. They belong to the 'Tests and Model Benchmarks' tour step and are the clearest executable description of how `oauth.dart` is meant to behave.

sections.title: Imports and fake JWT
sections.explanation: `_jwt` builds a token shaped like `x.<payload>.sig` with a base64url-encoded, unpadded claims payload. That is enough for the client, because `_idClaims` only decodes the middle part and never checks the signature.

sections.title: Fake browser
sections.explanation: `fakeBrowser` plays the browser and the provider. It hands the auth URL to an `inspect` callback, then requests the `redirect_uri` with `code` (or `error`) and the original or tampered `state`. The request runs fire-and-forget, so the app cannot assume the callback arrives after `openBrowser` returns. Because it always rewrites the host to `127.0.0.1`, the IPv6 `localhost` listener in `oauth.dart` is not covered by these tests.

sections.title: Google happy path
sections.explanation: Checks the authorization URL (host, client ID, mail scope, `access_type=offline`, S256, 127.0.0.1 redirect, login hint). The key PKCE check hashes the `code_verifier` sent to the token endpoint and compares it to the `code_challenge` in the browser URL. It also checks that the secret and the same redirect URI were sent, and that email, name and tokens were read back.

sections.title: Microsoft differences
sections.explanation: Checks the Microsoft-specific behavior: a `localhost` redirect, IMAP/SMTP/`offline_access` scopes, *no* `client_secret` in the token request, email taken from `preferred_username`, and Office 365 SMTP port 587.

sections.title: Failure paths
sections.explanation: The first test tampers with `state` and expects an `OAuthException` (the CSRF protection). The second sends `error=access_denied` and checks the friendly 'cancelled or not allowed' message. Its name says 'admin-consent errors from universities', but it actually tests the access-denied branch. The AADSTS admin-consent mapping in `_describeError` is not tested.

sections.title: Refresh keeps the old token
sections.explanation: Checks that `refresh` sends a `refresh_token` grant and, when the provider response has no new refresh token, keeps the old one (`fallbackRefresh`). Without that, the stored token would lose its refresh token and the user would be signed out.

OAUTH_SETUP.md.overview: A user guide for registering your own free Google and Microsoft OAuth apps so Hearthmail can sign in without passwords. It explains which method suits which kind of account and gives step-by-step console instructions, including common university problems. Its settings must match the code in `lib/services/oauth.dart` (scopes, redirect URIs, public client without a secret for Microsoft). It is the documentation part of the 'Sign-In: OAuth and Keychain' tour step.

sections.title: Why and which method
sections.explanation: Explains the main constraint: there is no company behind Hearthmail to register a shared OAuth app, so each user registers their own once per provider. The table recommends app passwords for personal Gmail, iCloud, Yahoo and Fastmail, and OAuth for university Google/Microsoft 365 and Outlook.com accounts, where app passwords are often unavailable.

sections.title: Google registration
sections.explanation: Steps to create a project, enable the Gmail API, configure an External consent screen with test users, and create a **Desktop app** client ID and secret. The Desktop-app client type is what allows the loopback `127.0.0.1` redirect used in `oauth.dart`. The notes cover the 'unverified app' warning, weekly re-sign-in in Testing mode (avoided by Publishing), and university admin blocks, which map to the `org_internal` error text in code.

sections.title: Microsoft registration
sections.explanation: Steps to register a multi-tenant app with a **Public client** redirect of `http://localhost` (matching the code's Microsoft redirect), add the `IMAP.AccessAsUser.All` and `SMTP.Send` delegated permissions, and allow public client flows, so no secret is needed. The notes explain 'Need admin approval' (the AADSTS65001 mapping in `_describeError`) and universities that disable IMAP or SMTP AUTH, which no client can work around.

sections.title: Privacy
sections.explanation: States that the password is never seen by the app, tokens are stored in the Keychain and refreshed automatically, and removing an account deletes its key (`SettingsStore.deletePassword` removes the `oauth.<id>` entry). It links to the providers' revocation pages. Note: the Google client *secret* entered in settings is stored in preferences rather than the Keychain. This document treats that secret as not truly secret.

FEATURES.md.overview: A feature matrix comparing Hearthmail with Apple Mail and Gmail, using status markers for built, possible, limited and impossible. It also records which local Ollama model handles which job, based on `tool/model_bench.dart`. It is the project's statement of scope and the best place to learn *why* some features are missing (most are limits of IMAP or of running without a server). It goes with the README in the 'Project Overview' tour step.

sections.title: Title and legend
sections.explanation: Dated status snapshot (17 Nov 2026) with a four-symbol legend. The ⚠️ 'possible with limits' category usually means 'works only while this app is running on this computer'.

sections.title: Reading and organizing
sections.explanation: Lists reading features and where each idea comes from. Most AI features (categories, priority, needs-reply, phishing warning) run on the local model; see `lib/models/triage.dart`. Snooze is ⚠️ because it is stored locally, and other devices still show the email. Server-side rules and closed-app notifications are ❌ because Hearthmail has no backend and Gmail filters cannot be reached over IMAP. Thread view is 🔜 although thread detection already exists for Mute.

sections.title: Writing and sending
sections.explanation: Composer features: AI writing tools, quick replies, Markdown sent as HTML, templates, signatures, undo send (5 to 30 s, matching `undoSendSeconds`). 'Send later' is ⚠️ because the app itself sends the message, so the computer must be on with the app open. Read receipts, confidential mode, Hide My Email and similar features are ❌ because they depend on closed provider services.

sections.title: Search
sections.explanation: Four search tiers: server keyword search, natural-language search turned into filters by the AI (`search_plan.dart`), semantic vector search, and 'ask your inbox' answers (the `_SearchHeader` answer card in `message_list.dart`). Offline full-text search is 🔜 because the local index stores meaning vectors, not text.

sections.title: Model choices from benchmarks
sections.explanation: Gives one model per job with measured results from `tool/model_bench.dart` on an M3 Pro: gemma4:12b-mlx for sorting and writing, embeddinggemma:300m for search, and translategemma:4b for reading translations. qwen3.6 was faster at writing but used more memory and sorted less accurately, so it is not recommended. This is why `AppSettings` has separate fast, writing, embedding and translation model fields.

sections.title: How semantic search works
sections.explanation: Each email (subject, sender, date, first 1,500 characters) becomes a 512-dimension embeddinggemma vector, stored per account in about 2 KB per email. A query is an exact linear scan (~10 ms for 20k emails), combined with server keyword results and reranked by the AI. The design choice is stated directly: no vector database is needed at this size. Background indexing depth (3,000) matches the `indexDepth` default in `AppSettings`.

lib/models/triage.dart.overview: The data model for AI triage: a `MailCategory` enum, a `MailPriority` enum and the `Triage` result class that the local model assigns to each email. It is small but central. Smart inbox views, list tags, sidebar categories and the phishing banner all read it, and it is saved to the triage cache as JSON. It belongs to the 'Domain Models' and 'Smart Inbox Triage' tour steps.

sections.title: MailCategory enum with prompt text
sections.explanation: An enhanced enum where each value has a UI `label` and a `description`. The description reads like guidance for the AI ('bills, banks, receipts…'), so it is presumably used to build the triage prompt; that keeps the UI and prompt definitions in one place. The `notification` value shows as 'Updates', so `name` (used for storage and AI output) and `label` (shown in the UI) differ. `parse` falls back to `other` for unknown or null strings, so an unexpected model output cannot crash the app.

sections.title: MailPriority enum
sections.explanation: Three levels with a tolerant `parse` that defaults to `normal`. These names are the strings the model returns (compare the `['high','normal','low']` enum in `tool/model_bench.dart`'s JSON schema).

sections.title: Triage value and JSON
sections.explanation: An immutable result with category, priority, `needsReply` and an optional `suspicious` flag. `toJson` writes `suspicious` only when true, using collection-if, so cached entries stay small and older cache files without the key still read as `false`. `fromJson` uses `== true` checks instead of casts, so missing or wrongly typed values become `false` rather than throwing. That makes the cache robust to schema changes.

android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml.overview: The Android app manifest, mostly the Flutter template. It declares the INTERNET permission, the app label, the single `MainActivity` that hosts Flutter, and the text-processing query Flutter needs. Its one significant change is `android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"`. It belongs to the 'Platform Config and Entitlements' tour step, next to the macOS entitlements that handle the same network questions on the main desktop target.

sections.title: Permissions and application flags
sections.explanation: `INTERNET` is required for IMAP, SMTP, OAuth and Ollama. `usesCleartextTraffic="true"` allows plain `http://` connections, which the default Ollama URL (`http://localhost:11434`, or a LAN IP from a phone) needs. Risk: it allows cleartext HTTP to *every* host app-wide. A `networkSecurityConfig` that allows cleartext only for local and Ollama hosts would be narrower.

sections.title: MainActivity
sections.explanation: Standard Flutter activity configuration: `singleTop` launch mode, a long `configChanges` list so Flutter handles rotation, resizing and theme changes itself without the activity being recreated, hardware acceleration, and `adjustResize` so the keyboard resizes the window (this matters for the composer and search field). The `NormalTheme` meta-data sets the window background behind Flutter after the launch theme.

sections.title: Embedding metadata and queries
sections.explanation: `flutterEmbedding=2` tells the Flutter tool to generate the v2 plugin registrant; it must not be removed. The `<queries>` block declares package visibility for `PROCESS_TEXT` intents (Android 11+), which Flutter's text-processing plugin uses for selection actions.

README.md.overview: The project README is the front door: it explains that Hearthmail is a Flutter email client whose AI runs entirely through a local Ollama server, so no email content leaves the machine. It maps every AI feature to where it appears in the UI, lists the Ollama models to pull, describes multi-account sign-in, and sketches the `lib/` layout. Tour step 1 uses it as the feature map that later steps implement one row at a time.

sections.title: Title and privacy promise
sections.explanation: States the two defining constraints of the project: all AI goes through [Ollama](https://ollama.com) on the local computer, and one Flutter codebase targets macOS, Windows, Android and iOS. The privacy claim ("no email content leaves your computer") is the design driver behind the pluggable `AiProvider` layer and the on-disk caches you will see later.

sections.title: AI feature map
sections.explanation: A Markdown table pairs each AI feature (Smart inbox, Summarize, Quick replies, AI search, Catch me up, Search by meaning, Translate, Phishing warning, ...) with the UI surface that hosts it: sidebar, reading pane, composer or search bar. Use it as an index: Smart inbox maps to `sidebar.dart` and `triage_cache.dart`, AI search to `search_plan.dart`, and so on. The paragraph after the table lists the non-AI Apple Mail/Gmail features, and the last lines note that the composer sends light Markdown as HTML with a plain-text fallback, which is implemented in `MailService.build`.

sections.title: Running on macOS
sections.explanation: Lists the build prerequisites (Xcode, Flutter, Ollama) and the three models with their roles: `gemma4:12b` for sorting/summaries/writing, `embeddinggemma:300m` for semantic search and the optional `translategemma:4b`. These names show up again as defaults and as helper text in the Settings page model pickers.

sections.title: Accounts and sign-in
sections.explanation: Explains that multiple accounts stay connected at once and merge into **All Inboxes**, with each message colored by account (the `accountColor`/`AccountBadge` helpers in `sidebar.dart`). It names the three sign-in paths (Google OAuth, Microsoft OAuth, app password with autodetection or autoconfig), which correspond exactly to the chooser in `account_setup_page.dart`. Note the README says secrets go to the macOS Keychain; on other platforms that depends on `flutter_secure_storage` behaviour.

sections.title: Project layout
sections.explanation: A compact tree of the most important source files. Notably, the AI layer under `services/ai/` is described as "independent of Flutter and the mail code", which is why `EmailContent` exists as a library-neutral model. `mail_service.dart` is described as "one per account, operations serialized", the key concurrency property explained in step 6.

sections.title: Other platforms, tests, license
sections.explanation: Phones cannot run Ollama, so the suggested approach is to point the Ollama address setting at a Mac on the LAN (started with `OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0`) or implement another `AiProvider`. Be aware that exposing Ollama on `0.0.0.0` makes it reachable to anyone on that network and that the traffic is plain HTTP, which partly weakens the "nothing leaves your computer" promise. The tests section distinguishes offline unit tests from the live `tool/ai_smoke.dart` check.

lib/models/email_content.dart.overview: A tiny, immutable value class carrying the facts about one email that the AI needs: id, sender, recipients, subject, date, body and unread state. It deliberately has no dependency on `enough_mail`, so the AI layer (`email_ai.dart`) can be reused and unit-tested without a mail server. `MailService.toContent` is the adapter that converts a `MimeMessage` into this shape. It is one of the domain models introduced in tour step 4.

sections.title: Constructor and fields
sections.explanation: A `const` constructor with required identity fields and optional `to`, `date` and `isUnread`. The `id` doc comment matters: it is the stable key used to cache AI results, which `MailService.keyOf` derives from the Message-ID header (falling back to `mailbox#uid`). All fields are `final`, so instances are safe to share between isolates of work and caches.

sections.title: Snippet for previews
sections.explanation: Collapses all whitespace runs into single spaces and clips at 280 characters with an ellipsis. This is a cheap, pure getter, but note it recomputes the regex replacement on every call; callers that read it in hot paths (list rendering) pay that cost each time.

sections.title: Prompt rendering with truncation
sections.explanation: `forPrompt` renders the email as a header block plus body, which is the text actually fed to the local model. Bodies over `maxBodyChars` (12,000 by default) are cut and tagged with `[…email truncated…]` so one huge newsletter cannot overflow the model's context window. Collection-`if` elements omit `To:` and `Date:` when absent, keeping prompts compact; the date is converted with `toLocal()` so the model reasons in the user's timezone.

lib/services/triage_cache.dart.overview: Persists AI triage results (category, priority, needs-reply) per message so each email is sorted by the model only once. There is one JSON file per account in the application support directory, plus an in-memory variant for tests. It backs the Smart inbox views that the sidebar shows in tour step 8: without it, every launch would re-run the local model over the whole inbox.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Uses `dart:io` for file access, `dart:convert` for JSON and `path_provider` to locate the platform's application support directory. Only the `Triage` model is imported from the app, keeping the cache independent of UI and state.

sections.title: Constructors and storage fields
sections.explanation: A private constructor is used by `open`, while `TriageCache.memory` creates a cache with a `null` file so nothing is ever written: a simple way to make tests and previews side-effect free. The initial data is copied with a spread (`{...data}`) so the caller's const map is never mutated.

sections.title: Opening the per-account file
sections.explanation: The account id is sanitized (anything outside `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` becomes `_`) before being used in the file name, preventing path tricks from addresses containing `/` or `..`. Note two different addresses could sanitize to the same name (e.g. `a.b@x` vs `a_b@x`), which would share a cache; harmless here because keys are Message-IDs. Corrupt JSON is swallowed on purpose: the comment says the only cost is a re-sort.

sections.title: Lookup operators
sections.explanation: An index operator and `contains` give map-like reads without exposing the underlying `Map`, so all writes are forced through `putAll` where persistence happens.

sections.title: Batch write with eviction
sections.explanation: Entries are merged, then the map is trimmed to 5,000 by removing the first keys in iteration order. Dart's default `Map` is a `LinkedHashMap`, so this evicts the oldest *inserted* keys; re-sorting an existing key does not refresh its position, so it is FIFO rather than true LRU. Every call rewrites the whole file with `writeAsString`, which is fine at this size but is not atomic: a crash mid-write could leave truncated JSON, which `open` then treats as a corrupt cache. Concurrent `putAll` calls are not serialized either.

sections.title: Clearing the cache
sections.explanation: Empties memory and deletes the file, used when the user forces a full re-sort or removes an account. Copying `_file` into a local variable enables Dart's null-promotion, since fields cannot be promoted directly.

lib/services/ai/ai_provider.dart.overview: Defines the seam between Hearthmail and any AI backend: an abstract `AiProvider` with model listing, streaming chat (optionally JSON-schema constrained) and embeddings, plus message/exception types. An extension adds `complete` and `completeJson` helpers that collect the stream. `OllamaProvider` implements it today, and the README suggests implementing it again for on-device phone models; this is the core of tour step 5's pluggable local AI layer.

sections.title: The AiProvider interface
sections.explanation: Three capabilities define a backend: `listModels`, `chat` returning a `Stream<String>` of chunks (so UI can show text as it arrives), and `embed`. `embed` has a default body that throws, so a provider without embedding support still compiles and semantic search simply reports it as unavailable. `close` is a no-op hook for releasing HTTP clients. The `jsonSchema` parameter lets callers ask the backend for structured output, which Ollama supports natively.

sections.title: Roles and messages
sections.explanation: `AiRole` mirrors the familiar system/user/assistant chat roles, and `AiMessage` offers named `const` constructors (`AiMessage.system(...)`) so prompt code reads naturally and allocates nothing at runtime for constant prompts.

sections.title: AiException
sections.explanation: A simple exception whose `toString` returns only the message, so it can be shown directly in the UI (for instance the sidebar's "AI offline" banner) without a class-name prefix.

sections.title: complete: whole-reply helper
sections.explanation: An extension method on `AiProvider`, so every implementation gets it for free without inheritance. It drains the stream into a `StringBuffer` and trims the result. Because it is an extension, implementations cannot override it, which keeps behaviour consistent across backends.

sections.title: completeJson: tolerant JSON decoding
sections.explanation: Requests a schema-constrained reply at a low temperature (0.1) for determinism, then decodes it. If strict decoding fails, it falls back to slicing from the first `{` to the last `}`, rescuing models that wrap JSON in prose or code fences. The fallback can still throw a raw `FormatException` (not an `AiException`) if the slice is invalid, and the `as Map<String, dynamic>` cast will throw if the model returns a JSON array; callers should be prepared for both. Consumers such as `SearchPlan.fromJson` add their own defensive parsing on top.

lib/models/search_plan.dart.overview: `SearchPlan` is the structured form of a natural-language search: the AI turns "invoices from Acme last month" into keywords, sender, dates and flags. The class then compiles that plan into two server query languages: standard IMAP SEARCH (RFC 3501) and Gmail's X-GM-RAW syntax. It is a domain model in tour step 4 and the bridge between the AI and the mail server in the AI search flow of step 9.

sections.title: Fields and constructor
sections.explanation: Every criterion is optional; defaults are an empty keyword list and `false` flags, so an empty plan means "recent mail". Keeping this a plain immutable value lets it be logged, compared and described without touching the network.

sections.title: Defensive JSON parsing
sections.explanation: `fromJson` assumes the model's output may be sloppy: the local `str` helper rejects non-strings, blanks and the literal string `"null"` (a common LLM habit), and `date` uses `DateTime.tryParse` so a bad date silently drops the filter instead of throwing. Keywords are trimmed and filtered, and booleans only count when they are exactly `true`. This is a good pattern for any model-produced JSON: validate field by field rather than trusting the schema.

sections.title: withoutKeywords and isEmpty
sections.explanation: `withoutKeywords` produces a relaxed plan, presumably used to retry a search when keyword matching is too strict. Notice it also drops `subject`, not just keywords; that may be intentional (subject is text-like) but is easy to miss. `isEmpty` checks every criterion and drives the decision in `MailService.search` to fall back from Gmail syntax to plain IMAP.

sections.title: Human-readable description
sections.explanation: Builds the line shown above search results (for example `about "invoice", from acme, after 2026-10-01`) so the user can see how the AI interpreted the question. Showing the interpreted plan is an important transparency feature when a model, not the user, writes the query.

sections.title: Compiling to IMAP SEARCH
sections.explanation: Maps each criterion to an RFC 3501 key (`FROM`, `SINCE`, `UNSEEN`, ...). IMAP `OR` is binary, so multiple keywords are folded right-to-left into nested `OR TEXT a OR TEXT b TEXT c` and parenthesized. `hasAttachment` is silently ignored here because standard IMAP has no attachment search key, so non-Gmail accounts may return more results than the description suggests. An empty plan becomes `ALL`.

sections.title: Compiling to Gmail query
sections.explanation: The same plan rendered in Gmail's search language (`from:`, `after:yyyy/mm/dd`, `is:starred`, `has:attachment`), which supports attachments and ranks better than plain IMAP on Gmail. Keywords are OR-ed inside parentheses. `MailService.search` later wraps this in `X-GM-RAW "..."` and re-escapes quotes.

sections.title: Quoting and date helpers
sections.explanation: `_q` produces an IMAP quoted string, escaping backslashes and double quotes so user/AI text cannot break out of the string. `_g` quotes multi-word Gmail terms but simply strips embedded quotes. `_imapDate` formats `d-Mon-yyyy` as RFC 3501 requires (English month names regardless of locale), and `_ymd` zero-pads for Gmail and display.

lib/services/mail_service.dart.overview: `MailService` is the single gateway to one account's mail server: IMAP for reading and organizing, SMTP for sending, built on `enough_mail`'s `MailClient`. Its central design rule is that every IMAP operation is serialized through a promise chain and re-selects its folder, because IMAP state (the selected mailbox) is connection-wide. It also hosts static helpers that turn `MimeMessage`s into display strings, AI-ready `EmailContent`, unsubscribe info, phishing hints and thread keys. This is the main file of tour step 6 and is reused by sending in step 12.

sections.title: Imports and credential types
sections.explanation: `MailCredentials` is a Dart 3 `sealed` class with two subclasses, so the `switch` in `_account` is checked for exhaustiveness at compile time. `OAuthCredentials` carries the token, the `OAuthClient` able to refresh it, and an optional `onTokenRefreshed` callback so refreshed tokens can be written back to the Keychain.

sections.title: Constructing the MailClient
sections.explanation: The doc comment explains the core risk the class guards against: a background Inbox refresh slipping between "select Sent" and "delete message 12". The `MailClient` is configured to download whole messages up to 256 KB so previews and AI sorting avoid extra round trips, with 30s response / 10s write timeouts. For OAuth accounts it wires `refresh` to the OAuth client and `onConfigChanged` to persist the refreshed token; for passwords both are `null`.

sections.title: Mapping config to MailAccount
sections.explanation: A `switch` expression with object patterns (`PasswordCredentials(:final password)`) destructures the credentials and builds either a password-based or XOAUTH2-based `MailAccount`. TLS mode is chosen per direction: implicit TLS (`ssl`) unless the config says STARTTLS. `outgoingClientDomain: 'localhost'` avoids leaking the machine's hostname in the SMTP EHLO greeting. `me` is the `From` address used when building outgoing mail.

sections.title: Serialization and reconnect
sections.explanation: `_serial` chains each operation onto `_tail`, so operations run strictly one at a time; the tail swallows errors (`onError: (_) {}`) so one failure does not poison the queue, while the caller still receives the original error. On anything that *looks* like connection loss (matched by exception type or message substrings such as `closed`), it reconnects once and retries. The substring heuristic is broad: a server error mentioning "closed" would also trigger a reconnect and a retry, which for non-idempotent operations like `moveMessage` could act twice. `_ensure` skips a redundant SELECT when the right mailbox is already selected.

sections.title: Listing folders and pages
sections.explanation: `mailboxes` asks for a sensible order (Inbox, Starred, Drafts, Sent, ...) and hides non-selectable container folders. `fetchPage` always re-selects to get a fresh message count, computes the page bound, and fetches with `fullWhenWithinSize`, then sorts by date descending because server sequence order is not guaranteed to match date order. `ensureFull` lazily downloads bodies that were too large, using a longer 60s timeout.

sections.title: Server-side search
sections.explanation: `searchFolder` prefers Gmail's All Mail so search covers archived mail. `search` drops to the low-level `ImapClient` to send either `X-GM-RAW "..."` on Gmail or the RFC 3501 criteria from `SearchPlan`, using UID search for stable ids. Only the highest `limit` UIDs (roughly newest) are fetched. The Gmail branch strips backslashes and escapes quotes before embedding the query, guarding against IMAP command injection from AI-produced text.

sections.title: Flag and move operations
sections.explanation: Each mutation runs inside `_serial` and calls `_ensure(box)` first, the pattern the class comment motivates. `archive` moves to the Archive folder or, on Gmail, All Mail, which mimics Gmail's own Archive by removing the Inbox label; `junk` and `moveToInbox` resolve targets by special-use flags. `fetchPart` returns a locally cached attachment when available and only goes to the network otherwise. The local `MimeMessage` flags (`isSeen`, `isFlagged`) are updated after the server call so the UI reflects the change.

sections.title: Building and sending mail
sections.explanation: `build` renders Markdown to HTML (GitHub-flavoured extension set) and a plain-text alternative, choosing multipart/mixed when there are attachments. Replies use `originalMessage` when the source message is loaded, or explicit `In-Reply-To`/`References` headers for scheduled sends (note the Dart 3.8 null-aware element `?references`). `addBinary` uses `readAsBytesSync`, which blocks the UI isolate for large attachments. `sendBuilt` marks the original as answered afterwards but ignores failures, since the send itself already succeeded.

sections.title: Background index fetch
sections.explanation: `fetchRange` walks the mailbox backwards by sequence number (newest first, skipping `skip`), optionally envelope-only, for the semantic search indexer. The comment notes the indexer uses its own connection, so it does not block the interactive queue on the main `MailService`.

sections.title: Static message helpers
sections.explanation: Pure helpers shared by UI and AI: subject/sender formatting, `bodyText` (cached per message in an `Expando`, so the cache dies with the message and never leaks), `keyOf` for stable AI cache keys, and `toContent` producing `EmailContent`. `unsubscribeOf` parses RFC 2369/8058 headers and only allows one-click over HTTPS. `suspicionOf` is a lightweight phishing heuristic (a display name containing a different address, or a brand name not matching the domain); it can false-positive on legitimate third-party senders mentioning a brand. `threadKeyOf` groups conversations by first `References` id, then `In-Reply-To`, then Message-ID, falling back to a normalized subject that strips multilingual reply prefixes (Re, Fwd, AW, SV, ...).

lib/services/user_data.dart.overview: Stores the user's personal mail organization on the device: VIPs, blocked senders, muted threads, snoozes ("Remind me"), follow-up reminders, scheduled "Send later" messages, templates, per-account signatures and an autocomplete contact book. Everything is serialized as one JSON blob in `SharedPreferences` under a versioned key. It is the data layer behind the local organization features in tour step 13 and is edited directly by the Settings page.

sections.title: Snooze record
sections.explanation: A snoozed message keeps its cache key, account, due time and subject, plus the folder `path` and `uid` so it can be brought back even if it is no longer loaded in memory. `isDue` uses `!isBefore` so a snooze due exactly now counts as due. `fromJson` tolerates missing optional fields with `?? ''` defaults, which keeps older saved data loadable after new fields are added.

sections.title: FollowUp record
sections.explanation: Represents a sent message to chase if nobody replies by `due`. The JSON keys are short (`id`, `account`) and differ from the Dart field names, so renaming fields in code does not break stored data.

sections.title: ScheduledMail record
sections.explanation: Everything needed to send a message later without the composer: recipients as strings, body, threading headers (`inReplyToId`, `references`) and attachment file paths. This matches the `inReplyToId`/`references` parameters of `MailService.build`. Two risks: the full body is stored in plaintext `SharedPreferences`, and attachments are stored as paths, so a file moved or deleted before send time will fail.

sections.title: Template record
sections.explanation: A minimal named body for reusable replies, with fully defaulted parsing.

sections.title: Opening and in-memory state
sections.explanation: `open` reads the JSON blob and silently ignores parse errors, meaning corrupt data resets to empty rather than crashing the app (at the cost of silently losing the user's lists). `UserData.memory()` has no prefs, so `save` becomes a no-op in tests. The public fields are mutable collections that `AppState` and the Settings page modify directly; contacts use a Dart record `(String, int)` for name and usage count.

sections.title: Load and serialize
sections.explanation: `_load` and `toJson` are mirror images, mapping each collection to a JSON list or map. Records are not JSON-encodable, so contacts are stored as two-element lists `[name, count]` and rebuilt on load. Note `_load` uses `addAll`, so calling it twice would merge rather than replace.

sections.title: Saving with a bounded contact list
sections.explanation: Before writing, contacts beyond 3,000 are pruned by lowest usage count, keeping the stored blob bounded. The whole object is re-encoded on every save; the Settings page calls `save` on every keystroke in a signature field, so this is frequent but cheap at this size.

sections.title: Rules and autocomplete
sections.explanation: `isBlocked` matches either the exact address or an `@domain` entry, which is how domain-wide blocking works. `noteContact` ignores no-reply style addresses and accumulates a weight per address, preserving an earlier name if the new one is blank. `suggestContacts` matches the prefix against the address or any word of the name and ranks by usage count; it scans all contacts each time, which is fine for at most 3,000 entries.

lib/ui/sidebar.dart.overview: The sidebar is the app's navigation column: unified inbox, special views (VIPs, Reminders, Scheduled, Follow up), the AI Smart inbox views (Priority, Needs reply, one entry per category) and an expandable list of accounts and their folders. It watches `AppState` and calls its methods to switch views, so it holds almost no state of its own. It is where the Smart inbox triage of tour step 8 becomes visible, and it also exports small color/icon helpers reused elsewhere.

sections.title: Category colors
sections.explanation: An exhaustive `switch` expression maps each `MailCategory` to a fixed color, so adding a category without a color is a compile error. These colors are reused for category dots in the sidebar and badges in message lists.

sections.title: Account colors and folder icons
sections.explanation: `accountColor` cycles through eight colors by index, giving each account a stable dot in merged lists (wrapping after eight accounts, so the ninth repeats the first). `mailboxIcon` picks an icon from IMAP special-use flags rather than folder names, so it works across languages and providers.

sections.title: Widget and local state
sections.explanation: `Sidebar` is stateful only to remember which accounts are expanded (`_expanded`). The optional `onNavigate` callback lets the phone layout close its drawer after a tap, keeping the widget layout-agnostic. The expanded set is not persisted, so it resets on each launch.

sections.title: Row builders
sections.explanation: Inside `build`, local functions `item`, `icon`, `dot` and `header` act as tiny private widgets sharing the theme. `item` wraps every tap so `onNavigate` always fires after the action. `?trailing` is Dart's null-aware collection element: the trailing widget is included only when non-null.

sections.title: Unified and special views
sections.explanation: `usedCategories` is built with an `if-case` pattern so only categories actually assigned to current inbox mail are listed, avoiding empty views. Special views appear only when their data exists (e.g. Reminders only with snoozes). Each entry compares `state.view` against a `const MailView` value, which works because `MailView` implements value equality; counts come from `state.unreadFor`. Note `usedCategories` is recomputed on every rebuild by calling `triageOf` for every inbox message.

sections.title: Smart inbox section
sections.explanation: Shown only when the local AI is ready. The header shows live progress (`Sorting x/y`) while `state.sorting`, otherwise a ✨ button that forces a full re-sort via `sortInboxes(force: true)`, bypassing the triage cache. Priority and Needs reply are fixed entries, followed by one entry per used category in enum order.

sections.title: Accounts and folders
sections.explanation: The Accounts header pushes `AccountSetupPage` to add another account. Each account row toggles expansion, and its trailing widget reflects connection status with a `switch` on `ConnectionStatus`: a spinner while connecting, an error icon that retries on tap, or an expand chevron. Expanded accounts list their folders indented; tapping one calls `state.openFolder`. Unread counts are only computed from loaded inbox messages, so they reflect the fetched page, not the server total.

sections.title: AI offline banner
sections.explanation: When `aiError` is set, a warning row is pinned below the list with a Retry button wired directly to `state.refreshAi`. Keeping it at the bottom outside the `ListView` keeps it visible regardless of scroll.

sections.title: AccountBadge widget
sections.explanation: A small dot-plus-email label used in merged message lists to show which account a message belongs to, reusing `accountColor` so colors match the sidebar.

lib/ui/settings_page.dart.overview: The Settings screen collects every user preference: Ollama address and model choices, semantic search and index depth, translation, undo-send delay and signatures, VIPs and blocked senders, writing style, inbox behaviour, OAuth client registrations and account removal. It reads and writes through `AppState` (`updateSettings` with immutable `copyWith` snapshots) and edits `UserData` collections directly. It is the UI half of tour step 13.

sections.title: Imports and widget
sections.explanation: A standard `StatefulWidget`, needed because the page owns several `TextEditingController`s. `material_ui` is the Material widget import the project uses throughout the UI.

sections.title: Controllers and lifecycle
sections.explanation: `late final` fields are initialized lazily on first access, which lets them use `context.read<AppState>()` without an `initState`. The signature controllers are built once from the accounts present when the page opened; an account added while Settings is open gets no signature field (the later `if-case` safely skips it). `dispose` cleans up every controller, and `_save` is a one-line funnel to `AppState.updateSettings`.

sections.title: Build setup and helpers
sections.explanation: The page watches `AppState` so status and model lists update live. Model lists are filtered with `AppState.isChatModel`/`isEmbeddingModel` and a name check for `translategemma`. `modelPicker` only sets `initialValue` when the saved model is installed, avoiding a Dropdown assertion error for unknown values, and disables itself when no models exist.

sections.title: Local AI section
sections.explanation: Shows connection status and lets the user change the Ollama address. The Reconnect button saves the URL if it changed (which reconnects through settings) or else calls `refreshAi`, guarding with `_checking` and a `mounted` check after the await. Separate fast and writing models let users trade quality for memory, as the helper text notes.

sections.title: Search section
sections.explanation: Toggles semantic search and explains why it may be unavailable (no embedding model installed). Changing index depth saves and immediately re-runs `indexAll`; Rebuild is disabled while indexing. The depth dropdown falls back to 3000 when the stored value is not one of the offered choices.

sections.title: Translation and sending
sections.explanation: `'auto'` is used as a sentinel for the translation model, displayed as "Automatic" or "Same as writing model". Undo-send offers fixed delays. Signatures write straight into `state.userData.signatures` and call `save()` on every keystroke without notifying listeners, which is acceptable because only this page shows them, but it bypasses `AppState`'s usual mutation path.

sections.title: People and writing style
sections.explanation: VIP and blocked lists are rendered as deletable chips calling `toggleVip`/`unblock` on `AppState`. Name and style notes save on every change; the style notes feed AI writing prompts so drafts match the user's voice.

sections.title: Inbox and sign-in apps
sections.explanation: Switches for automatic AI sorting and remote image loading (off by default blocks tracking pixels). The sign-in fields store the user's own Google/Microsoft OAuth client IDs. Note these use `state.settings.copyWith` while other sections use the `s` snapshot from build time; both work, but mixing them is a subtle inconsistency. The Google secret is obscured here but not on the account setup page.

sections.title: Accounts section
sections.explanation: Lists each account with a status icon and a subtitle built from a nested `switch` on `AuthType`. Removal is guarded by a confirmation dialog that clarifies mail stays on the server, then calls `state.removeAccount`. An Add account button pushes `AccountSetupPage`.

lib/ui/account_setup_page.dart.overview: The account setup screen handles all three ways to add a mailbox: Sign in with Google, Sign in with Microsoft (both OAuth via the user's own app registration) and app password with provider presets or automatic server discovery. Every path builds an `AccountConfig`, verifies it with `AppState.testAccount` before saving, and then calls `addAccount`, which stores secrets in the Keychain. It is used as the first-run screen and as a pushed page, and is the UI half of tour step 7.

sections.title: Widget and form state
sections.explanation: `isFirstRun` switches between a welcome layout with no AppBar and a normal pushed page. State holds controllers for the password form, a detected `ProviderPreset`, busy/discovering flags, the chosen `_method` (null while choosing) and OAuth client fields. `dispose` loops over every controller, an easy-to-maintain pattern.

sections.title: Presets and server discovery
sections.explanation: As the email is typed, `ProviderPreset.forEmail` fills known servers instantly. For unknown domains, `_discover` (run when the email field loses focus) uses `enough_mail`'s `Discover`, which queries Mozilla's ISP database, autoconfig and DNS, and opens the advanced section if nothing is found. `_lastDiscovered` prevents repeating the network lookup for the same address, and every `setState` after an await is guarded by `mounted`.

sections.title: Password sign-in flow
sections.explanation: Validates input, falls back to discovery if hosts are empty, builds an `AccountConfig` with the lowercase email as id, and tests the connection before saving. Spaces are removed from app passwords only for known presets, since providers like Gmail display them grouped. Risks: after discovery it only re-checks the IMAP host, so an empty SMTP host can slip through; and if `addAccount` throws, `_busy` is never reset, leaving the button disabled.

sections.title: OAuth client registration
sections.explanation: Hearthmail has no company server, so each user registers their own OAuth app. `_hasClient` checks whether an ID is saved, and `_saveClient` persists it (plus a client secret for Google desktop apps) through `updateSettings`. There is no `mounted` check before the final `setState`.

sections.title: OAuth sign-in flow
sections.explanation: Opens the browser via `client.signIn` (PKCE plus loopback redirect, per the README), then builds a config from the provider's fixed servers and the returned email/name, and tests IMAP/SMTP with `OAuthCredentials`. Microsoft failures get an extra explanation because some organizations disable IMAP for Microsoft 365. On success the token is saved with `addAccount`, and the user's name is adopted for AI signatures if none is set. All errors are mapped through `AppState.friendlyError`.

sections.title: Sign-in method chooser
sections.explanation: Builds three large outlined buttons using a local `option` helper. Selecting one sets `_method` and clears any previous client ID/secret input so a half-entered Google secret is not reused for Microsoft.

sections.title: OAuth panel
sections.explanation: If no client is registered, it shows numbered, selectable setup steps for Google Cloud or Microsoft Entra with a link to the console, and fields to paste the IDs. Once registered, it shows a Continue in browser button whose label reflects waiting/connecting states, plus a way to clear and change the registration. `?error` uses the null-aware collection element to insert the error only when present. The Google client secret field here is not `obscureText`, unlike in Settings.

sections.title: Page layout and password form
sections.explanation: `build` composes the welcome header, then whichever panel matches `_method`. The password form wraps fields in an `AutofillGroup` so system password managers can help, and triggers discovery when the email field loses focus. The help box shows preset-specific instructions and uses an `if-case` object pattern (`ProviderPreset(passwordUrl: final url?)`) to show a link only when the preset has one. The collapsible server settings show host/port fields with a reminder of the common TLS ports.

tool/ai_smoke.dart.overview: Developer smoke-test script (dart run tool/ai_smoke.dart [model]) that exercises every EmailAi feature live against the local Ollama server using six realistic sample emails and a fixed clock, printing each result with timing and setting a failing exit code on errors.

ios/Runner/Info.plist.overview: iOS bundle Info.plist for the Runner app: display name "Hearthmail", Flutter build name/number versioning, scene-based lifecycle via SceneDelegate, launch storyboard and supported orientations for iPhone and iPad.

macos/Runner/Info.plist.overview: macOS bundle Info.plist for the Runner app, filling bundle name, identifier, copyright and minimum system version from xcconfig variables and Flutter build name/number.
